Practical Marketing Science A field guide to measuring what marketing actually does Christos Visvardis October 2026 Preface This book is for people whose job is to answer a deceptively simple question: what did our marketing actually do? You might sit in a growth team, an analytics team, an agency or a consultancy. You probably already know how to write SQL, fit a regression and read a confidence interval. What tends to be missing is not technique but judgment: which method fits which question, what each method can and cannot tell you, and how to turn a model output into a budget decision someone will act on. That is the gap this book tries to close. How this book is organized The book is organized around the decisions a measurement team supports, not around techniques. Most chapters follow the same shape: The decision the chapter supports, stated up front. The method, explained just far enough to use it correctly. A worked example on simulated data, so you can see the method recover (or fail to recover) a known truth. Pitfalls: the ways the method goes wrong in practice and how to spot them. A checklist to run before you trust a result. Further reading, an annotated selection from the resource library in Appendix A. Simulated data is a deliberate choice. With real data you never know the true answer, so you cannot tell whether a method worked. With simulated data you set the truth yourself and then check what the method recovers. Every example in the book is reproducible from the code shown. Contents at a glance The parts build on each other but can be read out of order: each chapter states the decision it supports and points back to the earlier material it relies on. Part Chapters I. Chapter 1 What marketing science is for Whether a measurement effort is worth doing at all, which evidence to trust when sources disagree, and how to organize a measurement program so that it keeps feeding budget decisions instead of producing reports nobody acts on. 1.1 Measurement exists to change decisions Marketing science is not the production of numbers. It is the reduction of uncertainty around decisions that cost money. If a measurement cannot plausibly change what someone does, it is not worth its cost, however elegant it is. Marketing teams make four kinds of decisions, and each needs a different kind of evidence: Decision Typical question Evidence that answers it Precision needed Level How much should we spend in total next quarter? Marketing mix model, aggregate experiments Low to medium Allocation Where should the next euro go? Response curves, marginal returns by channel and market Medium Keep or kill Does this channel or tactic work at all? Incrementality experiment Medium to high Execution Which creative, audience or bid strategy? A/B tests inside a platform, platform reporting Relative ranking only Two things follow from this table. First, no single method answers all four. An MMM is good at level and allocation, poor at creative choice. A platform A/B test is good at execution, silent on whether the channel is incremental at all. Second, the precision you need depends on the decision. If a channels return would have to fall by half before you changed its budget, an estimate within plus or minus 30% is already enough. Spending another quarter to tighten that interval is wasted effort. This is the idea of value of information: a measurement is worth what it saves you in expected bad decisions. A practical version of it is to ask, before any analysis, what would we do differently if the answer came out high, and what if it came out low? If both answers lead to the same action, skip the analysis. 1.2 Three numbers that get confused Most arguments about marketing performance are really arguments between three different quantities that share the same name. Quantity Definition Where it comes from What it is good for Attributed Conversions a tracking rule assigns to a channel Platform reporting, analytics tools, multi-touch attribution Relative comparisons within a channel; operational optimization Incremental (average) Conversions that would not have happened without the channel, divided over its total spend Experiments, well-identified models Keep-or-kill decisions; checking whether a channel works at all Marginal Extra conversions from the next unit of spend Response curves from MMM or dose-response experiments Allocation and budget level Attributed and incremental numbers can differ by an order of magnitude. Average and marginal numbers differ whenever returns diminish, which is almost always. A channel can have an excellent average incremental return and a terrible marginal one because it is already saturated. Budget decisions are made at the margin, so the marginal number is the one that matters for allocation, and it is also the one hardest to measure. 1.3 Worked example: how attribution flatters retargeting To see how far apart attributed and incremental numbers can be, we simulate a market where we know the truth. Each of 200,000 users has a baseline probability of converting with no advertising at all. Two channels run: Retargeting reaches users who have already shown interest, so its audience is selected on intent. It raises conversion probability by a true 0.4 percentage points. Prospecting reaches users roughly at random and raises conversion probability by a true 1.0 percentage point. Conversions are credited with a last-touch rule: if a user saw both, retargeting gets the credit because it comes later in the journey. import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 200_000 intent = rng.beta(1, 30, n) # baseline conversion probability (mean ~3%) # retargeting is selected on intent; prospecting reaches people roughly at random exposed_rt = rng.random(n) < np.clip(intent * 6, 0, 0.9) exposed_pr = rng.random(n) < 0.25 LIFT_RT, LIFT_PR = 0.004, 0.010 # true absolute lifts u = rng.random(n) # one draw per user, reused for the counterfactuals def converts(rt_on=True, pr_on=True): p = intent + LIFT_RT * exposed_rt * rt_on + LIFT_PR * exposed_pr * pr_on return u < p actual = converts() incremental = { "Retargeting": actual.sum() - converts(rt_on=False).sum(), "Prospecting": actual.sum() - converts(pr_on=False).sum(), } attributed = { # last touch: retargeting wins whenever both touched the user "Retargeting": (actual & exposed_rt).sum(), "Prospecting": (actual & exposed_pr & ~exposed_rt).sum(), } spend = {"Retargeting": 30_000, "Prospecting": 60_000} tbl = pd.DataFrame({"Spend (EUR)": spend, "Attributed conv.": attributed, "Incremental conv.": incremental}) tbl["Attributed CPA"] = (tbl["Spend (EUR)"] / tbl["Attributed conv."]).round(0) tbl["Incremental CPA"] = (tbl["Spend (EUR)"] / tbl["Incremental conv."]).round(0) tbl["Attributed / incr."] = (tbl["Attributed conv."] / tbl["Incremental conv."]).round(1) print(tbl.T.to_string()) # transposed to fit the page ## Retargeting Prospecting ## Spend (EUR) 30000.0 60000.0 ## Attributed conv. 2662.0 1395.0 ## Incremental conv. 154.0 508.0 ## Attributed CPA 11.0 43.0 ## Incremental CPA 195.0 118.0 ## Attributed / incr. 17.3 2.7 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4)) x = np.arange(2) ax.bar(x - 0.18, tbl["Attributed CPA"], 0.36, label="Attributed CPA") ax.bar(x + 0.18, tbl["Incremental CPA"], 0.36, label="Incremental CPA (true)") ax.set_xticks(x, tbl.index) ax.set_ylabel("Cost per conversion (EUR)") ax.set_yscale("log") ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1), ncol=2) ax.set_title("Same campaigns, two very different answers") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 1.1: Attributed versus incremental CPA in the simulated market. Attribution ranks the channels in the wrong order. Attribution makes retargeting look like the cheapest channel by a wide margin. In truth it is the most expensive per incremental conversion. Nothing in the attribution rule is broken; it does exactly what it says. The problem is that retargetings audience would have converted at a high rate anyway, and last-touch credits all of those conversions to the last ad they saw. Any channel whose targeting is correlated with existing purchase intent (retargeting, branded search, CRM to engaged users, affiliates with coupon sites) will look better in attribution than it is. The general lesson: attribution measures who was touched before converting, not who was persuaded to convert. Only a comparison against a counterfactual can measure the second. Presenting platform-reported ROAS or attributed CPA as if it were incremental. Platform numbers are useful for comparing ad sets within a platform, where the selection bias is roughly constant. They are not evidence that a channel pays for itself. 1.4 An evidence hierarchy Because different sources answer different questions with different biases, a measurement program needs an explicit rule for which source wins when they disagree. One useful version, sometimes called the BEATS framework, ranks five layers from most to least authoritative: Business outcomes: revenue, accounts, margin, blended CAC from finance or the data warehouse. This is ground truth for what happened but says nothing about why. Experiments: holdouts, geo tests, conversion lift studies. The strongest evidence for causality, but narrow in time and scope. Analytics and models: marketing mix models, leading indicators such as branded search and site traffic. Broad coverage, but every causal claim rests on modeling assumptions. Tracking: pixels, platform attribution, multi-touch attribution. Granular and fast, but measures correlation with conversion paths. Surveys: self-reported attribution (how did you hear about us?). Useful for channels tracking cannot see (podcasts, word of mouth, offline), but subject to recall bias. The ranking is about authority, not usefulness. Lower layers are faster, cheaper and more granular, which is why you use them day to day. The ranking tells you what to do when they conflict: a survey never overrides the finance numbers, and a model never overrides a well-run experiment on the same question. When a model and an experiment disagree, the right move is usually to recalibrate the model toward the experiment (Chapter 11), not to average the two. Layer Answers Latency Granularity Main bias Business outcomes What happened in total Days to months Low None for totals; no causal attribution Experiments Did X cause Y, here, now Weeks Low to medium External validity (time, market, scale) Models How much did each driver contribute Weeks Medium Specification and confounding Tracking Who touched what before converting Real time High Selection on intent; signal loss Surveys What customers remember Days Medium Recall and salience 1.5 Triangulation: agreement and divergence When all layers tell the same story (blended CAC fell, an experiment shows good incremental CAC, leading indicators are up, platform CPAs fell, and more survey respondents name the channel), you can act with confidence. The interesting cases are divergences, and each pattern points to a specific diagnosis: Platform says up, business says flat. The platform is probably claiming credit for conversions that would have happened anyway, or modeled conversions have changed. Check for a tracking or attribution-window change before anything else. Experiment says strong, model says weak. The model may be under-crediting the channel because its spend is collinear with another driver, or the experiment ran in an unrepresentative period or market. Recalibrate the model with the experiment and check whether the test conditions match normal operation. Model says strong, nothing else does. Be suspicious. A channel whose spend rises with seasonal demand can absorb credit for the season (Chapter 3). Look for a test that can confirm it. Survey says strong, tracking says weak. Often a channel tracking cannot see, such as podcasts, video, word of mouth or offline. This is a candidate for a geo test, not a reason to dismiss either source. Divergence is information. It tells you either that one source is broken or that you have learned something about how the channel works. 1.6 Running measurement as a program Individual analyses rarely change much. A program that keeps a small set of methods in a feedback loop does. A minimal operating model has four parts: Always-on reporting from the business layer, cut by market and channel, with a log of every tracking change, naming change and promotion so that nobody compares across a break unknowingly (Chapter 2). A model (usually an MMM) refreshed on a fixed cadence, monthly or quarterly, used for level and allocation decisions. An experiment calendar that targets the models biggest uncertainties, not whatever a channel owner happens to want tested. A calibration loop: each experiment result is fed back into the model as a prior or constraint, and the models predictions are checked against the next experiment. Deciding what to test next is itself a prioritization problem. A simple scoring rule works well in practice: \[ \text{priority} \;\propto\; \text{spend} \times \text{uncertainty in incremental return} \times P(\text{result changes the budget}) \] A large channel with a well-established return scores low on uncertainty. A small channel scores low on spend. The best candidates are large channels whose incremental return nobody really knows, which in most companies means paid social prospecting, video and upper-funnel display. Measuring what is easy instead of what is uncertain. Teams often re-test paid search because it is easy to test, while the channels absorbing the most unexplained spend go untested for years. 1.7 Checklist What decision will this analysis inform, and who will make it? What would we do if the answer came out high? If it came out low? If both are the same, stop. Is the question about attributed, incremental or marginal performance? Is the method able to answer that question? Which evidence layer does the method belong to, and does a higher layer already disagree with it? What precision is needed for the decision, and can the planned design deliver it? Is there a tracking change, naming change or promotion in the window that would break a comparison? 1.8 Further reading Googles Measurement Playbook and Brand Measurement Playbook. Clear vendor-side statements of the experiment, model and attribution triad. Marketing attribution: a guided map (Sarahs newsletter). A good tour of how the attribution debate evolved. Kenneth Wilburs Advertising Measurement lecture slides. A rigorous academic overview of why observational ad measurement is hard. Decision making under contradictions (Carlos Agostini). How to act when models and experiments disagree. How to game attribution models (Admend, archived). A short, sobering list of the ways attribution rules can be exploited. VexPower simulations (e.g.iOS14 broke our tracking, Whats the impact of TV ads?). Hands-on case simulations for practicing these judgments. Full links are in Appendix A.

Chapter 2 Data and signal foundations Whether your data can support the analysis you are about to run. Most failed measurement projects fail here, quietly, long before any model is fitted. 2.1 The measurement dataset Almost every method in this book (MMM, geo tests, quasi-experiments, channel reporting) consumes the same underlying object: a panel of spend, delivery and outcomes by date, market and channel. Building that panel once, cleanly, and reusing it is the highest-leverage data work a measurement team can do. Field group Examples Notes Keys date, market (country, region, DMA), channel, sub-channel, campaign Fix the grain first. Daily by market by channel covers most needs. Spend media cost in a single currency, fees Agree whether agency and tech fees are included, and keep it constant. Delivery impressions, clicks, reach, GRPs Needed when spend and delivery decouple (CPM changes, auction shifts). Outcomes (system of record) sign-ups, accounts opened, first transactions, revenue From the backend or warehouse, not from pixels. Outcomes (tracked) platform conversions, analytics conversions Kept separately; used for diagnostics, never as the target. Controls price, promotions, product launches, holidays, competitor activity, macro indicators Anything else that moves the outcome. Events tracking changes, naming changes, outages, policy changes See the change log below. Two rules save a lot of pain. First, keep tracked and system-of-record outcomes in separate columns and never let one silently replace the other. Second, store the raw platform extracts and build the panel from them with versioned code, so that a mapping change can be replayed over history instead of only applying going forward. 2.2 Naming and taxonomy Channel-level analysis is only as good as the mapping from campaign to channel. A campaign called DE_Search_Brand_Q3 is easy; one called test_new_v2_final is not. A workable taxonomy has three properties: A naming convention enforced at creation, with fixed positions for market, channel, funnel stage, objective and audience, separated by a fixed delimiter. A mapping table for anything that does not follow the convention, owned by a named person and versioned. A fallback bucket (unmapped) that is monitored. If unmapped spend exceeds a small share of total spend, channel-level numbers are not reliable that week. Renaming or regrouping campaigns mid-period. If Paid Social is split into Prospecting and Retargeting in June, every year-on-year comparison at the sub-channel level is broken for twelve months unless history is remapped. 2.3 Tracked versus system-of-record outcomes Tracked outcomes come from pixels, SDKs and tags: they are what the ad platforms and web analytics tools see. System-of-record outcomes come from your own backend: accounts actually opened, payments actually received. The two diverge for many reasons, most of which have nothing to do with marketing: users decline consent or block trackers; the same person converts on a different device or browser than the one they clicked on; the platform models conversions it cannot observe and adds them to the count; attribution windows and counting rules differ between tools; tags break during site releases. Use the system of record as the outcome for every incrementality question. Use tracked outcomes for what they are good at: fast, granular, relative signals inside a channel. And monitor the ratio between the two, because a sudden change in that ratio is the most reliable early warning of a tracking problem. 2.4 Signal loss Since around 2020, the amount of user-level data available to measure advertising has fallen sharply, and it is not coming back. Mobile app tracking. Apples App Tracking Transparency (introduced with iOS 14.5) requires opt-in for cross-app tracking. Most users decline. App campaign measurement on iOS now runs largely through aggregated, delayed, privacy-thresholded postbacks. Browsers. Safari and Firefox block third-party cookies by default and limit the lifetime of some first-party cookies. Chromes plans have shifted several times; do not build a measurement strategy that depends on any browsers behavior staying fixed. Consent regimes. In the EU and UK, GDPR and ePrivacy rules mean a meaningful share of users never consent to marketing tags. Consent rates vary by country, by device and by banner design, which means tracking coverage itself varies by market. Modeled conversions. Platforms fill the gap with statistical models of the conversions they can no longer observe. The reported number is therefore partly a model output whose method you cannot inspect. The practical consequences are consistent. Platform-reported conversions are less complete and less comparable over time than they used to be. User-level methods such as multi-touch attribution have lost much of their input. Aggregate methods, which only need spend and outcomes by date and market, are largely unaffected. That is a large part of why marketing mix models and geo experiments have come back into fashion. 2.5 The change log Every analysis that compares two periods implicitly assumes nothing else changed between them. In practice something always did. A change log is a single table, maintained by the measurement team, recording every event that could break a comparison: Date Market Type Description Affects 2025-03-04 All Tracking New consent banner design Tracked conversions, all web channels 2025-04-15 DE Promo Spring bonus offer launched All outcomes in DE 2025-05-02 All Naming Paid social split into prospecting and retargeting Sub-channel reporting 2025-06-10 FR Outage Sign-up form errors for 6 hours Sign-ups in FR The log costs a few minutes a week and prevents the most common analytical error in marketing: attributing a change in a metric to a campaign when it was really caused by a tracking or product change in the same window. 2.6 Worked example: a campaign that seems to hurt We simulate a year of daily data for one market. The system of record (backend sign-ups) has a weekly pattern, mild growth and noise. On day 200 a new campaign launches that truly lifts sign-ups by 4%. Ten days earlier, on day 190, a consent banner change silently reduces the share of sign-ups the tracking tools can see by 12%. import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(7) days = np.arange(365) weekly = 1 + 0.15 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * days / 7) trend = 1 + 0.0004 * days campaign = np.where(days >= 200, 1.04, 1.0) # true +4% lift from day 200 backend = rng.poisson(400 * weekly * trend * campaign) # system of record coverage = np.where(days >= 190, 0.62, 0.70) # tracking coverage drops on day 190 tracked = rng.binomial(backend, coverage) df = pd.DataFrame({"day": days, "backend": backend, "tracked": tracked}) pre, post = df.query("170 <= day < 200"), df.query("200 <= day < 230") for col in ["tracked", "backend"]: change = post[col].mean() / pre[col].mean() - 1 print(f"{col:8s}: 30 days after vs 30 days before launch = {change:+.1%}") ## tracked : 30 days after vs 30 days before launch = -4.1% ## backend : 30 days after vs 30 days before launch = +3.4% Read on tracked conversions, a naive before-and-after comparison says the campaign coincided with a drop. Read on the backend, it says the opposite. Neither 30-day comparison is a valid estimate of the campaign effect (Chapter 3 explains why), but the tracked version is not even measuring the right thing. The tracking break is easy to find if you look at the ratio of tracked to backend outcomes. Below, a simple least-squares search finds the single day that best splits the ratio series into two segments with different means. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ratio = (df["tracked"] / df["backend"]).to_numpy() def best_split(x, min_seg=14): """Single change point minimizing within-segment squared error.""" costs = [((x[:k] - x[:k].mean())**2).sum() + ((x[k:] - x[k:].mean())**2).sum() for k in range(min_seg, len(x) - min_seg)] k = int(np.argmin(costs)) + min_seg return k, x[:k].mean(), x[k:].mean() k, before, after = best_split(ratio) print(f"Break detected at day {k}: ratio {before:.3f} -> {after:.3f}") ## Break detected at day 190: ratio 0.698 -> 0.620 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2)) ax.plot(days, ratio, lw=0.8, color="#6B6B6B", label="Daily tracked / backend") ax.hlines([before, after], [0, k], [k, 364], color="#1F4E79", lw=2, label="Segment means") ax.axvline(k, ls="--", color="#C8102E", lw=1.2, label="Detected break") ax.axvline(200, ls=":", color="#9A5B00", lw=1.5, label="Campaign launch") ax.set_xlabel("Day"); ax.set_ylabel("Ratio") ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8, ncol=2) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 2.1: Tracked-to-backend ratio. The detected break (dashed) lands on the consent change, ten days before the campaign launch (dotted). In real work, replace the toy search with a proper change-point library (the ruptures package in Python, changepoint in R) and run it as a scheduled check on the ratio for every market and channel. A break in the ratio does not tell you what happened, only where to look; the change log usually tells you the rest. 2.7 Checks before any analysis Before fitting anything, run a short battery of checks on the panel. Each one corresponds to a failure that has burned real projects. Check What you are looking for Typical cause Completeness Missing days, markets or channels; zero spend that should not be zero Failed extracts, API limits, new accounts not connected Duplicates The same spend counted twice Overlapping extracts, agency and platform reporting the same campaign Currency and time zone Spend jumps at month boundaries, conversions shifted by a day Mixed currencies, platform time zone differs from warehouse Unmapped share Spend not assigned to any channel New campaigns that break the naming convention Ratio stability Breaks in tracked / backend, clicks / impressions, spend / impressions Tracking changes, auction or pricing changes Outliers Single days far from the series Outages, bot traffic, data errors, real but one-off events Variation Channels whose spend barely moves Always-on channels; a model cannot learn their effect from history The last check matters more than it looks. A model can only learn the effect of a channel from variation in its spend. A channel that ran at the same level every week for two years has no variation to learn from, and no amount of modeling will fix that. The fix is to create variation on purpose, which is one of the strongest arguments for running experiments (Part II). 2.8 What to request for a model or a test When you start an MMM or plan a geo test, the data request is the first deliverable. A good request specifies: History. At least two years of weekly data for an MMM, three if you want to separate seasonality from trend with confidence. For a geo test, at least as many pre-period weeks as you plan to test, and preferably several times more. Grain. Weekly or daily, by the smallest geography at which media can be bought separately. Media. Spend and a delivery metric (impressions or GRPs) per channel, per geography, per period, including channels that are hard to collect such as TV, out-of-home, podcasts and sponsorships. Outcomes. The business outcome from the system of record, plus any intermediate outcome you want to model (site visits, sign-ups, activations). Controls. Prices, promotions, product changes, distribution changes, holidays, and any known external shocks. Events. The change log for the full period. Starting to model before the data request is complete. Missing channels do not disappear; their effect is absorbed by whichever included variable happens to be correlated with them, and the model gives that variable the credit. 2.9 Checklist Is the outcome taken from the system of record, not from tracking? Are tracked and backend outcomes stored side by side, with their ratio monitored? Is there a change log, and does any entry overlap the analysis window? Is unmapped spend below an agreed threshold for every week in the window? Have currency, time zone and duplicate checks been run? Does every channel you want to measure have enough spend variation to learn from? Are all channels included, including offline ones, so that omitted spend does not bias the rest? 2.10 Further reading Data request checklist and Marketing without cookies (Saxifrage). Chapter 3 Causal thinking for marketers Whether an observed relationship between marketing and outcomes can be read as an effect, what you need to control for (and what you must not control for), and which identification strategy a question needs before anyone opens a dataset. 3.1 Every marketing question is a counterfactual Did the campaign work? means how many conversions happened that would not have happened without it? The second half of that sentence describes a world that did not occur. Causal inference is the discipline of estimating outcomes in worlds you cannot observe. The standard notation makes this precise. For a unit \(i\) (a user, a market, a week) let \(Y_i(1)\) be the outcome with the campaign and \(Y_i(0)\) the outcome without it. The effect is \(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\). We only ever observe one of the two, which is called the fundamental problem of causal inference. Every method in this book is a different way of constructing a credible stand-in for the missing half: Randomized experiments make the stand-in a randomly chosen control group. Geo experiments and synthetic control make it a weighted combination of untreated markets. Difference-in-differences makes it the treated groups own past, adjusted by the trend in a comparison group. Regression and MMM make it a model prediction with the treatment set to zero. The methods differ in how much they rely on assumptions you cannot check. That is the axis on which to compare them, more than precision or convenience. 3.2 Why marketing data is especially confounded Marketing data is close to a worst case for naive analysis, because spend is rarely set independently of the outcome it is supposed to drive. Budgets follow demand. Planners spend more in peak season because that is when customers buy. Spend and sales rise together even if the ads do nothing. Targeting follows intent. Retargeting, branded search and CRM reach people who were already likely to convert (Chapter 1). Some channels respond to demand mechanically. Search spend rises when more people search, which happens when demand is high for any reason. Changes cluster. Campaigns launch with promotions, product releases and price changes. Before-and-after comparisons cannot separate them. Activity bias. People who are online a lot both see more ads and do more of everything online, including converting. Each of these creates a correlation between spend and outcomes that is not caused by the spend. The size of that spurious correlation is often larger than the true effect. 3.3 Drawing the problem: causal graphs A causal graph (a DAG, for directed acyclic graph) is a diagram of what causes what. Drawing one before analysis forces assumptions into the open, and it tells you exactly which variables to adjust for. Three patterns cover most situations. Figure 3.1: The three basic structures. Adjust for confounders; do not adjust for mediators when you want the total effect; never adjust for colliders. Forks. Seasonality drives both spend and sales. It is a confounder: you must adjust for it, or the seasonal pattern will be credited to spend. Chains. TV spend drives branded search, which drives sales. Branded search is a mediator: part of the TV effect flows through it. If you put branded search into the model as a control, you block that path and the model credits TV with only its direct effect. This is one of the most common errors in marketing mix models, and it systematically under-credits upper-funnel media. Colliders. Ad exposure and existing intent both make a user more likely to click. If you restrict your analysis to clickers, you create a spurious negative correlation between exposure and intent among the people you study. Any analysis that filters on a post-treatment outcome (users who engaged, visitors who reached the pricing page) risks collider bias. The rule that falls out is simple to state: adjust for common causes of treatment and outcome, do not adjust for anything the treatment itself affects. 3.4 Worked example: three regressions, three answers We simulate three years of weekly data in which the truth is known. Underlying demand has a strong annual cycle. Planners set spend from a seasonal forecast, so spend is higher in peak season. Spend raises branded search, which raises sales, and spend also has a direct effect on sales. The true total effect of one extra unit of spend is 8 sales: 2 directly plus 1.5  4 through branded search. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.formula.api as smf rng = np.random.default_rng(3) t = np.arange(156) season = 300 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 52) # forecastable seasonal demand demand = 1000 + season + rng.normal(0, 40, t.size) spend = 50 + 0.08 * season + rng.normal(0, 8, t.size) # planners spend into the peak brand_search = 200 + 4 * spend + 0.3 * demand + rng.normal(0, 15, t.size) sales = 0.5 * demand + 1.5 * brand_search + 2 * spend + rng.normal(0, 30, t.size) df = pd.DataFrame({"sales": sales, "spend": spend, "brand_search": brand_search, "s1": np.sin(2*np.pi*t/52), "c1": np.cos(2*np.pi*t/52)}) models = { "Naive: sales ~ spend": "sales ~ spend", "Adjusted: + seasonality": "sales ~ spend + s1 + c1", "Over-adjusted: + brand search": "sales ~ spend + s1 + c1 + brand_search", } rows = [] for name, f in models.items(): fit = smf.ols(f, df).fit() lo, hi = fit.conf_int().loc["spend"] rows.append({"Model": name, "Estimate": fit.params["spend"], "95% CI low": lo, "95% CI high": hi}) res = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Model").round(1) res["True effect"] = 8.0 print(res.to_string()) ## Estimate 95% CI low 95% CI high True effect ## Model ## Naive: sales ~ spend 17.5 16.7 18.3 8.0 ## Adjusted: + seasonality 8.4 7.2 9.6 8.0 ## Over-adjusted: + brand search -0.8 -2.3 0.6 8.0 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6)) y = np.arange(len(res))[::-1] err = [res["Estimate"] - res["95% CI low"], res["95% CI high"] - res["Estimate"]] ax.errorbar(res["Estimate"], y, xerr=err, fmt="o", color="#1F4E79", capsize=4) ax.axvline(8, color="#C8102E", ls="--", lw=1.2, label="True total effect") ax.set_yticks(y, res.index); ax.set_xlabel("Sales per unit of spend") ax.legend(loc="lower right") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 3.2: Estimated effect of spend under three specifications. Only the model that adjusts for the confounder and leaves the mediator alone recovers the truth. The naive regression roughly doubles the true effect, because spend rides on the seasonal peak and gets credit for it. Adding seasonal terms removes the confounding and lands near the truth with an interval that contains it. Adding branded search does something worse than expected. You might guess it would cut the estimate to the direct effect of 2, since it blocks the path through search. Instead the estimate falls to around zero. The reason is that branded search is not only a mediator: it is also driven by demand fluctuations the model cannot see. That makes it a collider between spend and unmeasured demand, and conditioning on it opens a spurious path that pushes the spend coefficient down further. In real data, where branded search responds to everything from news coverage to competitor activity, this is the normal situation, not a contrived one. Notice that all three regressions fit the data well and all three produce tight confidence intervals. Statistical precision tells you nothing about whether the specification is right. Only the causal structure, which comes from domain knowledge rather than from the data, tells you which estimate to believe. The example is also generous to the analyst in one respect: planners reacted only to the forecastable seasonal pattern, which the sine and cosine terms capture completely. If planners also reacted to unexpected demand (a competitor exits, a news story breaks), seasonal controls would not remove that part of the confounding, and the adjusted estimate would still be biased upward. That is the general weakness of adjustment methods: they only remove confounding you have measured. Including branded search, site visits or any other downstream metric as a control in a model meant to measure the total effect of upper-funnel media. If the variable sits between the media and the outcome, controlling for it removes part of the effect you are trying to measure. 3.5 A ladder of identification strategies Each strategy for estimating a causal effect rests on an assumption. The higher up the ladder, the weaker and more checkable the assumption. Strategy Key assumption How checkable Covered in Randomized experiment (user-level) Randomization was done correctly and nothing leaks between groups High: balance checks, A/A tests Chapter 5 Geo experiment Control markets would have followed the treated markets path Medium-high: pre-period fit Chapter 6 Synthetic control, CausalImpact Weighted controls track the treated unit, and no other shock hits it in the test window Medium: pre-period fit, placebo tests Chapter 7 Difference-in-differences Parallel trends between treated and comparison groups Medium: pre-trend checks Chapter 7 Regression adjustment, MMM All confounders are measured and the functional form is right Low: relies on domain knowledge Chapters 9 to 11 Raw correlation, before-and-after Nothing else changed Essentially none Avoid Two practical consequences. First, if a decision is large and the question can be answered with a method higher up the ladder, it usually should be. Second, when you must use a method lower down, say so in the readout and name the confounders you could not rule out. 3.6 Reporting an observational result honestly An observational analysis is not worthless; it is often the only option. But the reader needs to know what kind of evidence it is. A short template: Design. This is an observational before-and-after comparison with seasonal controls. It is not an experiment. Estimate with uncertainty. The point estimate, its interval, the sample size and the time window. Confounders not ruled out. A price change in week 14 and a competitors campaign in weeks 15 to 18 overlap the window and could explain part of the change. Direction of likely bias. Both would push the estimate up, so the true effect is more likely below the estimate than above it. What would settle it. A four-week geo holdout in two matched markets would give a direct estimate. 3.7 Checklist Have you written down the counterfactual: what exactly would have happened without the treatment? Have you drawn the causal graph, including how the budget was set? Which variables are confounders (adjust) and which are mediators or colliders (do not adjust)? Does the analysis filter on anything that happens after treatment? Where on the identification ladder does the method sit, and is the decision large enough to justify climbing higher? Does the readout state the design, the uncertainty and the confounders that remain? 3.8 Further reading Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Scott Cunningham) and Causal Inference for the Brave and True (Matheus Facure). The two most practical free introductions; the second is written in Python. Causal Inference in R (r-causal.org) and Applied Causal Inference Powered by ML and AI (causalml-book.org). Deeper treatments with code. Give the confounder its own equation (drmike.xyz). A clear argument for modeling how budgets are set, directly relevant to MMM. Chapter 4 Bayesian reasoning in practice How to express what you know about a marketing effect as a probability, how to combine evidence from different sources, and how to turn uncertainty into a decision instead of a significance verdict. 4.1 Why Bayesian thinking fits marketing This chapter is not an argument that every analysis should be Bayesian. Frequentist methods are fine, and many results in later chapters are reported with ordinary confidence intervals. It is an argument that the way of thinking fits marketing decisions unusually well, for four reasons. Stakeholders ask Bayesian questions. How likely is it that this channel pays for itself? is a question about the probability of a hypothesis given the data. A p-value answers a different question (the probability of data this extreme if the effect were zero), and the mismatch causes endless confusion. Prior knowledge exists and should be used. You usually know something before the data arrives: past experiments, industry benchmarks, the physical impossibility of a channel driving 300% of revenue. Ignoring it is not neutral; it is a choice to pretend you know nothing. Data is often small and noisy. Weekly data for a two-year MMM has about 100 observations and a dozen or more parameters. Priors are what keep such models from producing absurd answers. Evidence accumulates. A measurement program produces a stream of experiments and model refreshes. Bayesian updating gives a principled way to combine them instead of treating each one in isolation. The mechanics are compact. Start with a prior distribution over the quantity of interest. Combine it with the likelihood of the observed data. The result is the posterior, which is what you now believe. Every summary you report (an estimate, an interval, a probability that the effect exceeds a threshold) is read off the posterior. 4.2 Worked example: an A/B test, read two ways A landing page test runs with 12,000 users per arm. The control converts 360 users (3.00%) and the variant converts 402 (3.35%). The frequentist reading: import numpy as np from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest conv = np.array([402, 360]); n = np.array([12_000, 12_000]) z, p = proportions_ztest(conv, n, alternative="two-sided") rel_lift = (conv[0] / n[0]) / (conv[1] / n[1]) - 1 print(f"Observed relative lift: {rel_lift:+.1%}, two-sided p = {p:.3f}") ## Observed relative lift: +11.7%, two-sided p = 0.122 The result is not significant at 5%, and in many organizations the conversation ends there, with the variant discarded. The Bayesian reading starts from a weak prior (Beta(1, 1), uniform over conversion rates) and draws from the posterior of each arm: rng = np.random.default_rng(11) draws = 200_000 post_a = rng.beta(1 + 360, 1 + 12_000 - 360, draws) # control post_b = rng.beta(1 + 402, 1 + 12_000 - 402, draws) # variant lift = post_b / post_a - 1 print(f"P(variant better than control) = {(post_b > post_a).mean():.1%}") ## P(variant better than control) = 93.9% print(f"Relative lift: median {np.median(lift):+.1%}, 95% interval " f"[{np.quantile(lift, .025):+.1%}, {np.quantile(lift, .975):+.1%}]") ## Relative lift: median +11.6%, 95% interval [-3.0%, +28.5%] # Expected loss: how much conversion rate we give up, on average, if we pick the wrong arm loss_ship_b = np.maximum(post_a - post_b, 0).mean() loss_keep_a = np.maximum(post_b - post_a, 0).mean() print(f"Expected loss if we ship the variant: {loss_ship_b*100:.3f} pp") ## Expected loss if we ship the variant: 0.006 pp print(f"Expected loss if we keep the control: {loss_keep_a*100:.3f} pp") ## Expected loss if we keep the control: 0.356 pp The data are identical; what changes is what you report. There is roughly a 94% chance the variant is better, the likely lift is around 12% but could plausibly be anywhere from slightly negative to nearly 30%, and the expected cost of shipping it if we are wrong is under a hundredth of a percentage point of conversion, while the expected cost of keeping the control is over a third of a point is a statement a product owner can act on. It also makes the real trade-off visible: if the variant is cheap to ship and easy to revert, a 94% probability with a small expected loss is a good bet; if shipping it is costly or irreversible, it may be worth running longer. Two cautions keep this honest. First, with a weak prior and a reasonable sample size, the Bayesian interval is numerically close to the frequentist one. The Bayesian framing does not create evidence that is not there. Second, the decision rule must be fixed before the test, exactly as with significance testing. Ship if the probability of being better exceeds 95% and expected loss is below X is a rule; looking at the posterior every day and stopping when it looks good is peeking, and it inflates false positives in Bayesian and frequentist analysis alike (Chapter 5). 4.3 Worked example: combining a model and an experiment A marketing mix model estimates the incremental return on ad spend (iROAS) of a paid social channel at 1.8, with posterior standard deviation 0.6. A geo experiment on the same channel then estimates 1.1, with standard error 0.3. Which do you believe? Neither on its own. If both estimates are roughly normal and measure the same quantity, the combined estimate weights each by its precision (the inverse of its variance): \[ \mu_{\text{post}} = \frac{\mu_1/\sigma_1^2 + \mu_2/\sigma_2^2}{1/\sigma_1^2 + 1/\sigma_2^2}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{post}} = \left(\frac{1}{\sigma_1^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma_2^2}\right)^{-1/2} \] from scipy import stats mmm = (1.8, 0.6); geo = (1.1, 0.3) prec = [1/mmm[1]**2, 1/geo[1]**2] mu = (mmm[0]*prec[0] + geo[0]*prec[1]) / sum(prec) sd = sum(prec) ** -0.5 for name, (m, s) in {"MMM alone": mmm, "Geo test alone": geo, "Combined": (mu, sd)}.items(): p_win = 1 - stats.norm.cdf(1, m, s) print(f"{name:15s} iROAS {m:.2f} (sd {s:.2f}) P(iROAS > 1) = {p_win:.0%}") ## MMM alone iROAS 1.80 (sd 0.60) P(iROAS > 1) = 91% ## Geo test alone iROAS 1.10 (sd 0.30) P(iROAS > 1) = 63% ## Combined iROAS 1.24 (sd 0.27) P(iROAS > 1) = 81% import matplotlib.pyplot as plt x = np.linspace(-0.5, 4, 600) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.9)) curves = [(mmm, "MMM", "--"), (geo, "Geo test", ":"), ((mu, sd), "Combined", "-")] for (m, s), lab, ls in curves: ax.plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x, m, s), ls=ls, lw=2, label=f"{lab}: {m:.2f}") ax.axvline(1, color="#6B6B6B", lw=0.8) ax.text(1.03, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, "break-even", fontsize=8) ax.set_xlabel("iROAS") ax.set_yticks([]) ax.legend() plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 4.1: Precision-weighted combination of a model estimate and an experiment. The experiment dominates because it is more precise. The combined estimate sits much closer to the experiment because the experiment is four times as precise. This is the core logic of calibrating an MMM with experiments (Chapter 11): the experiment becomes a prior, or a likelihood term, that pulls the models channel estimate toward what was measured directly. The formula assumes both numbers measure the same thing. In practice they often do not: the experiment ran in two markets for four weeks at a particular spend level, while the MMM coefficient is an average over two years and all markets. Before combining, check that the spend level, time period and outcome definition match closely enough. If they do not, the honest move is to model the difference (for example, by widening the experiments uncertainty to reflect the gap) rather than pretending it is not there. 4.4 Choosing priors Priors attract suspicion because they look subjective. In marketing models they are usually the opposite: they encode hard constraints everyone agrees on and stop the model from wandering into impossible territory. Three kinds are useful. Weakly informative priors rule out the absurd without favoring any particular plausible value. Example: a channels ROI is positive and very unlikely to exceed 20. Informative priors from evidence, such as a past experiment or a meta-analysis of similar channels. These should be documented with their source. Structural priors on things like how quickly an ad effect decays (adstock) or how fast returns saturate, where the data alone rarely pins down the answer. A useful habit is the prior predictive check: before seeing the data, simulate what the prior implies about observable quantities and ask whether that looks sane. Suppose a business spends 50,000 per week on media and makes 100,000 per week in revenue, and you are choosing a prior for the media coefficient. import pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(5) spend, revenue = 50_000, 100_000 priors = { "Normal(0, 10) on coefficient": rng.normal(0, 10, 100_000), "LogNormal(log 1, 0.5) on ROI": rng.lognormal(np.log(1.0), 0.5, 100_000), } rows = {} for name, beta in priors.items(): share = beta * spend / revenue # implied share of revenue driven by media rows[name] = {"5%": np.quantile(share, .05), "median": np.median(share), "95%": np.quantile(share, .95), "P(impossible)": ((share < 0) | (share > 1)).mean()} pct = (pd.DataFrame(rows).T * 100).round(0).astype(int).astype(str) + "%" print(pct.to_string()) # P(impossible): share below 0% or above 100% ## 5% median 95% P(impossible) ## Normal(0, 10) on coefficient -824% 1% 823% 92% ## LogNormal(log 1, 0.5) on ROI 22% 50% 114% 8% The uninformative Normal(0, 10) prior says it is entirely plausible that media drives minus 800% or plus 800% of revenue, and it puts over 90% of its mass on impossible values. It is not neutral; it is wrong. The lognormal prior on ROI keeps medias share between roughly 20% and 110% of revenue, which is still generous but at least physically possible, and it encodes the belief that advertising does not destroy revenue. The second habit is sensitivity analysis: refit with a meaningfully different reasonable prior and see whether the decision changes. If it does, the data are not strong enough to settle the question, and the honest conclusion is that you need more data or an experiment, not that you should pick the prior that gives the preferred answer. Choosing priors after seeing which answer they produce. Priors must be set and documented before the model is fitted, with a source for each informative one. Otherwise the prior is just a dial for producing the result someone wanted. 4.5 From uncertainty to decisions The point of a posterior is to make decisions, and a decision needs two ingredients a significance test does not provide: the size of the possible gain and loss, and how much each outcome matters. Consider a budget decision on the paid social channel from the example above, where break-even is an iROAS of 1. The combined posterior says the channel probably pays back, but not certainly. The expected value of an extra 100,000 in spend is \[ E[\text{profit}] = 100{,}000 \times (E[\text{iROAS}] - 1), \] and you can also compute the probability of losing money and the expected size of that loss. A useful habit is to report all three: expected gain, probability of loss, and expected loss if wrong. Two channels with the same 80% probability of being profitable can be very different bets if one has a long left tail. Bayesian decision analysis also gives a clean answer to should we test this?: run the experiment if the expected reduction in bad-decision losses exceeds the cost of the test (including the revenue lost in the holdout). This is the value of information idea from Chapter 1, made quantitative. 4.6 Checklist Are priors set and documented before fitting, with a source for each informative prior? Has a prior predictive check confirmed that the priors imply plausible outcomes? Has a sensitivity analysis shown whether a different reasonable prior changes the decision? When combining a model and an experiment, do they measure the same quantity (spend level, period, market, outcome)? Was the decision rule (thresholds on probability and expected loss) fixed before looking at results? Does the readout report probability of loss and expected loss, not just a point estimate? 4.7 Further reading Bayes Rules! (Johnson, Ott and Dogucu) and Statistical Thinking for the 21st Century (Poldrack). Accessible introductions with code. bayesian-intro (Benjamin Rosenbaum, GitHub). A compact, practical course. priorsense (n-kall, GitHub). Tools for prior sensitivity analysis. Geometric intuition for MMM (Daniel Saunders). A visual explanation of how priors and data interact in Bayesian MMM. Calibration with experiments (Juan Orduz). The bridge from this chapter to Bayesian MMM calibration in Part III. Chapter 5 A/B tests that hold up Whether a change (a page, an offer, a message, an onboarding step) improved the outcome enough to ship, and how to design the test so that the answer is trustworthy whichever way it comes out. 5.1 Design before data An A/B test is the strongest evidence in marketing science because randomization breaks every confounding path at once. It is also the easiest to ruin, because every decision made after the data starts arriving is a chance to fool yourself. The fix is to write the design down before launch. A one-page test plan should fix: Element What to decide Common mistake Hypothesis What change, for whom, expected direction and mechanism Lets see what happens Randomization unit User, account, session, device, household Randomizing sessions when the outcome is per user Primary metric One metric that decides the test, defined precisely, with its window Picking the metric that moved after the fact Guardrail metrics Metrics that must not get worse (e.g.activation, complaints, unsubscribes) No guardrails, so a win damages something downstream Minimum detectable effect The smallest effect worth acting on Not computing it, then calling a null result a small positive lift Sample size and duration From the MDE, baseline rate and traffic; whole weeks Stopping when it looks significant Decision rule What result leads to ship, iterate or stop Deciding the rule after seeing the result Segments Which cuts will be examined, declared in advance Slicing until something is significant The plan does not have to be long. It has to exist before the data does. 5.2 Power and the minimum detectable effect The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is the smallest true effect the test has a good chance (usually 80%) of detecting at the chosen significance level. It is the single most useful number in test planning, because it tells you in advance what a null result will mean. For a conversion rate \(p\) and \(n\) users per arm, a good approximation of the relative MDE for a two-sided test at level \(\alpha\) with power \(1-\beta\) is \[ \text{MDE}_{\text{rel}} \approx \frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})\sqrt{2p(1-p)/n}}{p}. \] import numpy as np import pandas as pd from scipy import stats def rel_mde(p, n, alpha=0.05, power=0.8): z = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(power) return z * np.sqrt(2 * p * (1 - p) / n) / p ns = [5_000, 10_000, 25_000, 50_000, 100_000, 250_000] tbl = pd.DataFrame({f"baseline {p:.0%}": [rel_mde(p, n) for n in ns] for p in [0.01, 0.03, 0.10]}, index=pd.Index(ns, name="users per arm")) print((tbl * 100).round(1).astype(str).add("%").to_string()) ## baseline 1% baseline 3% baseline 10% ## users per arm ## 5000 55.8% 31.9% 16.8% ## 10000 39.4% 22.5% 11.9% ## 25000 24.9% 14.2% 7.5% ## 50000 17.6% 10.1% 5.3% ## 100000 12.5% 7.1% 3.8% ## 250000 7.9% 4.5% 2.4% Read the table before running any test. With 10,000 users per arm and a 3% baseline, the test can only reliably detect a relative lift of roughly 20% or more. Most real changes to a landing page move conversion by a few percent. Such a test is almost guaranteed to come back null, and when it does, the honest summary is we could not detect an effect; effects smaller than about 20% were undetectable with this sample, not no effect. Three levers improve the MDE, in roughly increasing order of usefulness: More traffic or a longer test. The MDE shrinks with the square root of the sample, so halving it takes four times the data. A metric closer to the change. A change to the pricing page is easier to detect on started sign-up than on first payment 60 days later, although the closer metric may not be the one you ultimately care about. Variance reduction (CUPED, below), which is often worth the equivalent of 20% to 50% more traffic for free. 5.3 Peeking: the most common way to ruin a test A fixed-sample test controls the false positive rate at 5% only if you look at the result once, at the planned end. If you check every day and stop as soon as the result is significant, the false positive rate climbs far above 5%. The simulation below runs 2,000 A/A tests, where there is no true difference, for 28 days and checks significance each day. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt rng = np.random.default_rng(1) sims, days, per_day, p = 2_000, 28, 500, 0.03 a = rng.binomial(per_day, p, (sims, days)).cumsum(1) b = rng.binomial(per_day, p, (sims, days)).cumsum(1) n = per_day * np.arange(1, days + 1) pooled = (a + b) / (2 * n) z = (b / n - a / n) / np.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * 2 / n) daily_sig = np.abs(z) > 1.96 fp_by_day = np.maximum.accumulate(daily_sig, axis=1).mean(0) # stopped at first "win" # Group sequential: 4 planned looks with O'Brien-Fleming boundaries looks = np.array([7, 14, 21, 28]) - 1 bounds = 2.024 * np.sqrt(4 / np.arange(1, 5)) fp_gs = (np.abs(z[:, looks]) > bounds).any(1).mean() print(f"Single look at day 28: {daily_sig[:, -1].mean():.1%}") ## Single look at day 28: 5.5% print(f"Daily peeking for 28 days: {fp_by_day[-1]:.1%}") ## Daily peeking for 28 days: 28.4% print(f"4 planned looks, OBF bounds: {fp_gs:.1%}") ## 4 planned looks, OBF bounds: 5.7% fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.9)) ax.plot(np.arange(1, days + 1), fp_by_day, lw=2, label="Stop at first significant daily look") ax.axhline(0.05, color="#C8102E", ls="--", lw=1, label="Nominal 5%") ax.set_xlabel("Days of peeking"); ax.set_ylabel("False positive rate") ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.matplotlib.ticker.PercentFormatter(1)) ax.legend(loc="upper left") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 5.1: False positive rate of A/A tests when stopping at the first significant daily look, compared with a single look at the end and with a four-look group sequential design. Daily peeking for four weeks turns a 5% false positive rate into something close to 30%: more than one in four winning tests is noise. The four-look group sequential design stays close to the nominal 5%. There are two honest fixes. Do not peek at the decision metric. Look at guardrails and data quality during the test, but decide only at the planned end. Plan the peeks. Group sequential designs fix a small number of interim looks in advance and use stricter thresholds at the early ones. OBrien-Fleming boundaries, used above, demand very strong evidence early and close to the usual threshold at the end, which keeps the overall error near 5% while still allowing an early stop for a large effect. Always-valid inference (mixture sequential tests) goes further and allows continuous monitoring, at some cost in power. If someone asks for an interim look at a fixed-sample test, give it, but say plainly that a significant interim result is not a reason to stop early under that design. 5.4 Multiple comparisons Every extra comparison is another chance for noise to look like a finding. If a test is read on one primary metric, three secondary metrics and five countries, that is up to 20 comparisons, and at a 5% threshold you should expect about one false positive even if nothing works. k = np.array([1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50]) print(pd.DataFrame({"comparisons": k, "P(at least one false positive)": (1 - 0.95 ** k).round(2)}).to_string(index=False)) ## comparisons P(at least one false positive) ## 1 0.05 ## 3 0.14 ## 5 0.23 ## 10 0.40 ## 20 0.64 ## 50 0.92 Practical rules: One primary metric decides. Everything else is supporting evidence or a guardrail. Declare segments in advance and correct for them. Holms method controls the chance of any false positive; the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controls the share of false discoveries and is less conservative. Both are one line with statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests. Treat unplanned segment findings as hypotheses for the next test, not as results. The variant worked in Italy only found after the fact is far more often noise than a real interaction. 5.5 Variance reduction with CUPED CUPED (controlled-experiment using pre-experiment data) uses a pre-period measure of the same metric to remove predictable variation from the outcome. If \(X\) is a users pre-period value and \(Y\) the in-test outcome, analyze \(Y - \theta(X - \bar X)\) with \(\theta = \text{cov}(X, Y)/\text{var}(X)\). Because \(X\) is measured before randomization, the adjustment cannot bias the estimate; it only shrinks the variance, by a factor of \(1 - \rho^2\) where \(\rho\) is the correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\). rng = np.random.default_rng(8) n = 20_000 pre = rng.gamma(2, 25, n) # pre-period spend per user treat = rng.random(n) < 0.5 post = 0.7 * pre + rng.gamma(2, 12, n) + 2.0 * treat # true effect: +2.0 per user theta = np.cov(pre, post)[0, 1] / pre.var() adj = post - theta * (pre - pre.mean()) for name, y in [("Raw", post), ("CUPED", adj)]: d = y[treat].mean() - y[~treat].mean() se = np.sqrt(y[treat].var() / treat.sum() + y[~treat].var() / (~treat).sum()) print(f"{name:6s} effect {d:5.2f} 95% CI [{d - 1.96*se:5.2f}, {d + 1.96*se:5.2f}] SE {se:.3f}") ## Raw effect 3.25 95% CI [ 2.42, 4.08] SE 0.423 ## CUPED effect 2.37 95% CI [ 1.90, 2.84] SE 0.242 print(f"Correlation pre/post: {np.corrcoef(pre, post)[0, 1]:.2f}") ## Correlation pre/post: 0.82 Two things happen. The CUPED standard error is a bit over half the raw one, which is equivalent to running the raw test with about three times the traffic. And the point estimate moves: in this particular sample the treatment arm happened to contain heavier spenders before the test started, which inflated the raw estimate well above the true 2.0. CUPED corrects for that chance imbalance and lands much closer to the truth. Randomization guarantees balance on average, not in every sample; CUPED fixes the sample you actually got. CUPED works best for metrics with stable individual behavior (spend, sessions, transactions) and does nothing for brand-new users with no history, which is a real limitation for acquisition tests. 5.6 Checks that catch broken tests Sample ratio mismatch (SRM). If the design splits traffic 50/50, the observed split should be close to 50/50. A significant deviation means something is wrong with assignment or logging (redirects that drop users, bot filtering applied to one arm, a variant that crashes on some browsers), and the result cannot be trusted whatever it shows. observed = np.array([50_600, 49_400]) chi2, p = stats.chisquare(observed) print(f"Split {observed[0] / observed.sum():.2%} / {observed[1] / observed.sum():.2%}: SRM p-value = {p:.5f}") ## Split 50.60% / 49.40%: SRM p-value = 0.00015 A 50.6/49.4 split looks harmless but is very unlikely by chance at this sample size. Investigate before reading the outcome. A/A tests. Running the testing setup with two identical arms is the cheapest way to verify that randomization, logging and analysis produce about 5% false positives. Run one whenever the tooling changes. Novelty and learning effects. A new design can win for two weeks because it is new, or lose for two weeks because users have to relearn something. Plot the daily effect; if it trends, the end-of-test average does not describe the long-run effect. Interference. If treated and control users interact (referrals, shared accounts, marketplaces, limited inventory), the control is contaminated and the estimate is biased. Randomize at a higher level (company, region) when this matters. Long outcome windows. Many marketing outcomes (activation, revenue, retention) arrive weeks or months after exposure. A test read at two weeks measures the short-term outcome only. When the decision depends on revenue or retention, define the readout as a cohort metric at a fixed horizon (for example 30, 60 or 90 days after assignment) and plan the timeline around it. Treating an ad platforms split test as an incrementality test. A platform A/B test compares two versions of an ad against each other; both arms are still advertising. It tells you which version performs better relative to the other, not whether either one causes conversions that would not have happened anyway. For that you need a holdout (Chapter 8) or a geo test (Chapter 6). 5.7 Tests before the product exists Some of the most valuable tests happen before anything is built. Smoke tests and fake doors present an offer, feature or product that does not exist yet and measure how many people try to take it. They size demand cheaply, at some cost in user trust if overused. Shadow brands run a test campaign under an unrelated brand name to measure response to an offer or positioning without exposing the main brand. Creative pre-testing with fractional factorial designs (sometimes called Taguchi or orthogonal-array testing) estimates the effect of several creative elements at once with far fewer cells than a full factorial, at the cost of assuming most interactions are small. 5.8 Reporting a test A readout that survives scrutiny reports, in this order: the decision and how confident it is; the design (unit, split, dates, sample size, primary metric and window); the estimate with its interval; the MDE the test had; guardrails; and any data quality issues found (SRM, logging gaps). A non-significant result is reported as we could not detect an effect larger than X, which is a real and useful result. 5.9 Checklist Is there a written plan with hypothesis, unit, primary metric and window, MDE, sample size, duration and decision rule, dated before launch? Does the MDE correspond to an effect size worth acting on? If not, redesign or do not run the test. Does the test run in whole weeks and long enough for the outcome window? Was the sample ratio checked, and were A/A tests run on this setup? Is the decision metric read only at the planned end, or under a pre-planned sequential design? How many comparisons does the readout make, and are they corrected or labeled as exploratory? Is a null result reported with the effect size that could have been detected? 5.10 Further reading Can we stop this test early? (VexPower simulation). A hands-on look at the peeking problem. Chapter 6 Geo experiments Whether a channel that cannot be randomized at the user level (TV, out-of-home, audio, paid social or search measured on business outcomes) is incremental, and by how much per euro, measured on the system-of-record outcome rather than on tracked conversions. 6.1 When geo tests are the right tool A geo experiment randomizes places instead of people. Some regions get a change in media (more, less or none) and the rest continue as usual. Because the outcome is measured as an aggregate per region and day, the method needs no user-level tracking at all. That makes it the natural choice when: the channel cannot be randomized at the user level (TV, radio, out-of-home, print); you want the outcome from your own backend, including offline and cross-device conversions, instead of the platforms tracked conversions; you want to check a platforms own lift study with an independent method (Chapter 8); you need an experiment to calibrate a marketing mix model (Chapter 11), which works at the same aggregate level. The price is statistical power. You have tens of units, not millions, and regions are noisy and different from each other. Most of the craft of geo testing is about getting enough power out of few, heterogeneous units. 6.2 Design choices Unit. The smallest geography at which media can be bought separately and outcomes can be measured reliably. In the US this is often the DMA. In Europe, whole countries are almost always too few and too different to serve as units; use administrative regions (NUTS-2 or NUTS-3), postal-code areas or commuting zones, which group areas where people live and work together and so reduce spillover. Number of units and treated share. More units means more power. With 30 to 60 regions, treating 20% to 50% of them is typical; the best split depends on how much of the business you are willing to put at risk. Assignment. Two approaches work: Stratified randomization: sort regions by size (or by a pre-period outcome), form blocks of similar regions, and randomly pick treated regions within each block. This keeps the design-based guarantee of randomization while balancing size. Matched selection: choose treated regions and controls to maximize pre-period similarity (as GeoLift and Googles matched markets tools do). It can increase power, but the guarantee now rests on the pre-period fit carrying over into the test period. Treatment type. Treatment What changes What it measures Go-dark holdout Media switched off in treated regions Average incremental return of current spend Heavy-up Extra spend in treated regions Marginal return of extra spend at the current level Scale-back (inverse) Spend reduced in treated regions Marginal return of the last units of spend These answer different questions. A go-dark test tells you whether the channel works at all; a heavy-up or scale-back tells you whether the next or last euro works, which is what an allocation decision needs (Chapter 1). Duration and cooldown. Long enough to accumulate power and to cover at least two full weekly cycles; for channels with long-lasting effects (TV, brand campaigns), add a cooldown period after the test during which the outcome is still measured, because effects persist after spend stops. 6.3 Worked example: a heavy-up test on 40 regions We simulate 120 days of daily conversions in 40 regions of very different sizes, with a shared weekly pattern, a shared trend, a national random walk and slow region-specific drift. After 90 pre-period days, 8 treated regions receive extra spend for 30 days, with a true lift of 6%. Assignment is stratified: regions are sorted by pre-period size into 8 blocks of 5, and one region per block is randomly treated. import numpy as np import pandas as pd from scipy.optimize import minimize rng = np.random.default_rng(21) G, T, T0 = 40, 120, 90 # regions, days, first test day t = np.arange(T) size = rng.lognormal(np.log(80), 0.7, G) # baseline daily conversions per region national = 1 + 0.12 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 7) + 0.0015 * t + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.006, T)) regional = 1 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.004, (G, T)), axis=1) # slow region-specific drift mu = size[:, None] * national[None, :] * regional # Stratified randomization: 8 blocks of 5 similar-sized regions, one treated per block pre_size = mu[:, :T0].mean(1) blocks = np.argsort(pre_size).reshape(8, 5) treated = np.array([rng.choice(b) for b in blocks]) is_t = np.isin(np.arange(G), treated) LIFT = 0.06 mu_obs = mu.copy() mu_obs[np.ix_(is_t, t >= T0)] *= 1 + LIFT y = rng.poisson(mu_obs).astype(float) print(f"Treated regions: {is_t.sum()}, share of pre-period conversions: " f"{y[is_t, :T0].sum() / y[:, :T0].sum():.0%}") ## Treated regions: 8, share of pre-period conversions: 19% The estimator is a synthetic control: a weighted combination of control regions, with non-negative weights summing to one, chosen to track the treated regions total as closely as possible in the pre-period. The test-period gap between the treated total and its synthetic twin is the effect estimate. def synth_effect(y, treated_mask, T0): target = y[treated_mask].sum(0) X = y[~treated_mask] X = X * (target[:T0].mean() / X[:, :T0].mean(1))[:, None] # put controls on treated scale k = X.shape[0] sse = lambda w: ((target[:T0] - w @ X[:, :T0]) ** 2).sum() w = minimize(sse, np.full(k, 1 / k), method="SLSQP", bounds=[(0, 1)] * k, constraints={"type": "eq", "fun": lambda w: w.sum() - 1}).x cf = w @ X lift = target[T0:].sum() / cf[T0:].sum() - 1 return lift, target, cf est, target, cf = synth_effect(y, is_t, T0) pre_mape = np.mean(np.abs(target[:T0] / cf[:T0] - 1)) print(f"Estimated lift: {est:+.1%} (true {LIFT:+.0%}); pre-period MAPE {pre_mape:.1%}") ## Estimated lift: +3.8% (true +6%); pre-period MAPE 3.4% A point estimate alone is not a result. To get its uncertainty we use placebo tests: repeat the exact same procedure many times on sets of 8 control regions that received no treatment. The spread of those placebo effects is the noise the method produces when the truth is zero. controls = np.where(~is_t)[0] placebo = [] for _ in range(300): fake = np.zeros(G, bool) fake[rng.choice(controls, 8, replace=False)] = True keep = ~is_t # truly treated regions excluded placebo.append(synth_effect(y[keep], fake[keep], T0)[0]) placebo = np.array(placebo) lo, hi = est - np.quantile(placebo, [0.975, 0.025]) p_val = (np.abs(placebo) >= abs(est)).mean() print(f"Lift {est:+.1%}, 95% interval [{lo:+.1%}, {hi:+.1%}], placebo p-value {p_val:.3f}") ## Lift +3.8%, 95% interval [+0.8%, +6.6%], placebo p-value 0.010 The estimate is below the true 6%, but the interval contains it and excludes zero. This is what one run of a sound design looks like: any single test lands somewhere in its interval, which is why the interval, not the point, is the result. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt roll = lambda s: pd.Series(s).rolling(7, center=True).mean() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3)) ax.plot(t, roll(target), lw=2, label="Treated regions") ax.plot(t, roll(cf), lw=2, ls="--", label="Synthetic control") ax.axvspan(T0, T - 1, color="#9A5B00", alpha=0.08, label="Test period") ax.set_xlabel("Day"); ax.set_ylabel("Daily conversions") ax.legend(loc="upper left") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 6.1: Treated regions (total) versus their synthetic control, 7-day averages. The gap after day 90 is the estimated effect of the heavy-up. 6.3.1 Power: what this design could have detected The same placebo distribution answers the planning question. If the true lift were \(L\), each placebo estimate would shift to roughly \((1+L)(1+e)-1\), where \(e\) is its null estimate, because the injected lift scales the treated total but not the synthetic control fitted on the pre-period. The power at \(L\) is the share of those shifted estimates that clear the critical value. crit = np.quantile(np.abs(placebo), 0.95) lifts = np.linspace(0, 0.10, 41) power = [(np.abs((1 + L) * (1 + placebo) - 1) > crit).mean() for L in lifts] mde = lifts[np.argmax(np.array(power) >= 0.8)] print(f"Critical |lift| at 5%: {crit:.1%}; MDE at 80% power: about {mde:.1%}") ## Critical |lift| at 5%: 2.9%; MDE at 80% power: about 4.2% fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6)) ax.plot(lifts * 100, power, lw=2) ax.axhline(0.8, ls=":", color="#6B6B6B") ax.set_xlabel("True lift (%)") ax.set_ylabel("Power") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 6.2: Power of the design by true lift, from the placebo distribution. The dotted line marks 80% power. In real work this analysis runs before the test, on historical data only: pick candidate treated sets, run placebos on the pre-period, and see whether the MDE is small enough to be worth the cost of the test. If it is not, change the design (more regions, longer duration, a bigger spend change) before spending any money. 6.3.2 From lift to iROAS The decision needs a return, not a lift. Suppose the heavy-up added 90,000 EUR of spend in the treated regions over the 30 days and each conversion is worth 120 EUR. extra_spend, value = 90_000, 120 cf_post = cf[T0:].sum() for label, L in [("estimate", est), ("95% low", lo), ("95% high", hi)]: incr = cf_post * L print(f"{label:9s} incremental conversions {incr:7.0f} iROAS {incr * value / extra_spend:4.2f}") ## estimate incremental conversions 1040 iROAS 1.39 ## 95% low incremental conversions 214 iROAS 0.29 ## 95% high incremental conversions 1804 iROAS 2.41 The point estimate says the heavy-up paid back, with an iROAS around 1.4. The interval runs from about 0.3 to 2.4, so the test cannot rule out that the extra spend lost money. That is a typical geo-test outcome and still useful: it rules out very high marginal returns, it gives a measured anchor that can be combined with a model estimate (Chapter 4), and it tells you how much bigger the next test would need to be to settle the question. What it does not support is a confident claim either way, and the readout should say so. 6.4 Analysis methods in practice Difference-in-differences ratio: the treated regions post/pre ratio divided by the controls post/pre ratio. Transparent, but sensitive to regions drifting apart. Synthetic control, as above, and its augmented variants (GeoLift uses an augmented synthetic control with a ridge correction for imperfect pre-period fit). Time-based regression (Googles GeoexperimentsResearch): regress the treated aggregate on the control aggregate in the pre-period and predict forward. Trimmed match (Google): a robust estimator for paired designs that trims the most extreme pairs, useful when a few regions behave very differently. With a good design, these methods usually agree within their uncertainty. When they disagree sharply, check the pre-period fit and look for a region with an unusual event during the test. Reading the test while it is running and extending it until it becomes significant. The peeking problem from Chapter 5 applies to geo tests too, and with few units it is worse. Fix the duration from the power analysis. 6.5 Things that break geo tests Spillover. People in control regions see the treated media (national TV, regional TV with overlapping coverage, people commuting into treated cities). Spillover biases the estimate toward zero. Commuting zones and buffer regions excluded from both groups reduce it. Imprecise geo-targeting. Digital platforms target by inferred location, which leaks across borders. Check delivery reports by region; a go-dark region still getting 15% of its normal impressions is a weaker treatment than designed. One region dominating. If one metropolitan region holds a third of the business, it will dominate both the treated total and the synthetic control. Consider splitting it, excluding it, or assigning it to control. Other changes during the test. A regional promotion, a sales team push, a local news story. Freeze other regional activity where possible and log anything that happens (Chapter 2). Unrepresentative timing. A test run in a seasonal low measures returns at low demand. Results transfer best to periods that look like the test period. 6.6 Checklist Is the geo unit the smallest one at which media and outcomes can both be separated, with spillover considered? Was assignment randomized (ideally stratified), and is the method fixed in advance? Does a pre-test power analysis on historical data give an MDE worth testing for? Is the treatment type (go-dark, heavy-up, scale-back) matched to the decision (average versus marginal return)? Is delivery verified by region, so that the treatment actually happened as designed? Is the outcome taken from the system of record, with a cooldown window for lasting effects? Is the result reported as an iROAS range from placebo-based or model-based intervals, with the MDE? 6.7 Further reading GeoLift (Meta) documentation, walkthrough and the Inverse GeoLift post.
