Chapter 7 Quasi-experiments: DiD, CausalImpact and synthetic control What an intervention that was not designed as an experiment actually did: a launch in one market, a price change, a site redesign, an SEO change, an outage, a campaign limited to some regions for operational reasons. 7.1 Making the best of things that already happened Most of the did X work? questions a measurement team receives are about things that already happened without a control group. You cannot randomize retroactively. What you can often do is find a comparison that plausibly shows what would have happened otherwise: other markets, other products, other customer groups, or the treated units own history adjusted for what happened to everyone else. These designs sit in the middle of the identification ladder (Chapter 3). They are much better than a raw before-and-after comparison and much weaker than a randomized test, because their key assumption, that the comparison would have moved like the treated unit, can be supported but never proven. 7.2 Difference-in-differences Difference-in-differences (DiD) compares the change in the treated group with the change in a comparison group over the same period. Anything that moved both groups equally (seasonality, macro conditions, a national campaign) cancels out. The key assumption is parallel trends: without the treatment, the two groups would have followed parallel paths. Parallel trends cannot be tested for the post-period, but it can be checked in the pre-period with an event study: estimate the treated-versus-control gap for each period relative to the treatment date. Before treatment, the gaps should hover around zero. After treatment, they trace out the effect over time. 7.2.1 Worked example: an event study Thirty regions are observed for 52 weeks. In week 30, ten of them get a new local sales and marketing program. The true effect builds up gradually, reaching 8% after four weeks. Outcomes are modeled in logs so that coefficients read as approximate percentage effects. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.formula.api as smf rng = np.random.default_rng(12) units, weeks, start = 30, 52, 30 treated = rng.choice(units, 10, replace=False) rows = [] unit_fe = rng.normal(np.log(500), 0.5, units) week_fe = 0.1 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(weeks) / 52) + 0.002 * np.arange(weeks) for u in range(units): for w in range(weeks): rel = w - start effect = min(0.02 * (rel + 1), 0.08) if (u in treated and rel >= 0) else 0.0 rows.append({"unit": u, "week": w, "treated": int(u in treated), "rel": rel, "log_y": unit_fe[u] + week_fe[w] + effect + rng.normal(0, 0.03)}) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) # Event-time dummies for treated units, binned at the ends; week -1 is the reference df["k"] = df["rel"].clip(-10, 15) for k in range(-10, 16): if k != -1: df[f"e{k + 10}"] = ((df["k"] == k) & (df["treated"] == 1)).astype(int) terms = " + ".join(c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("e") and c[1:].isdigit()) fit = smf.ols(f"log_y ~ C(unit) + C(week) + {terms}", df).fit( cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["unit"]}) es = pd.DataFrame({"k": [int(c[1:]) - 10 for c in terms.split(" + ")], "coef": [fit.params[c] for c in terms.split(" + ")], "se": [fit.bse[c] for c in terms.split(" + ")]}) pre = es[es.k < -1] print(f"Mean pre-period coefficient: {pre.coef.mean():+.3f} (max |coef| {pre.coef.abs().max():.3f})") ## Mean pre-period coefficient: -0.010 (max |coef| 0.025) print(f"Mean effect, weeks 4+ after start: {es[es.k >= 3].coef.mean():+.3f} (true +0.080)") ## Mean effect, weeks 4+ after start: +0.074 (true +0.080) import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.9)) ax.errorbar(es.k, es.coef, yerr=1.96 * es.se, fmt="o", ms=4, capsize=2, color="#1F4E79") ax.axhline(0, color="#6B6B6B", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(-0.5, color="#C8102E", ls="--", lw=1) ax.set_xlabel("Weeks relative to start (endpoints binned)"); ax.set_ylabel("Effect on log outcome") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 7.1: Event study: estimated treated-versus-control gap by week relative to the program start, with 95% intervals clustered by region. Flat pre-period coefficients support parallel trends. The pre-period coefficients sit around zero, the effect ramps up after the start and settles near the true 8%. Two features of the code matter in practice: standard errors are clustered by region, because weekly observations within a region are not independent, and the reference period is the week just before treatment. Staggered rollouts analyzed with an ordinary two-way fixed effects regression. When different units start treatment at different times and effects change over time, the standard regression compares late-treated units with already-treated units and can produce badly biased estimates, even with the wrong sign. Use estimators designed for staggered adoption (Callaway and SantAnna, Sun and Abraham, or the imputation approach), available in packages such as differences, diff-diff and DRDID. 7.3 CausalImpact: a model-based counterfactual When there is a single treated unit (one country, one product, the whole website) and several unaffected time series that move with it, a structural time series model can predict the counterfactual. This is the approach behind Googles CausalImpact package. The model is fitted on the pre-period, with the control series as regressors and a time-varying level to absorb slow drift, then projected through the post-period. The gap between actual and predicted is the effect, and the models forecast uncertainty gives its interval. The assumptions are specific and worth stating in any readout: The controls were not affected by the intervention. Other countries sign-ups are good controls for a country-specific change; branded search volume is a bad control for a campaign, because the campaign moves it. The relationship between the treated series and the controls is stable from the pre-period into the post-period. Nothing else happened to the treated unit alone during the post-period. 7.3.1 Worked example: a site change in one market A conversion-flow change goes live in one market on day 100 and truly lifts daily sign-ups by 10%. Three other markets, unaffected, serve as controls. import warnings, statsmodels.api as sm warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") rng = np.random.default_rng(5) T, T0 = 140, 100 t = np.arange(T) common = 100 + 0.15 * t + 8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 7) X = np.column_stack([common * a + rng.normal(0, 2.5, T) for a in (0.8, 1.1, 0.6)]) y = common + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.4, T)) + rng.normal(0, 2.5, T) y[T0:] *= 1.10 # true effect: +10% from day 100 def impact(y, X, T0, T1=None, reps=2000): """Fit on [0, T0), predict [T0, T1); return predicted mean, simulated paths.""" T1 = T1 or len(y) res = sm.tsa.UnobservedComponents(y[:T0], level="llevel", exog=X[:T0]).fit(disp=False) pred = res.get_forecast(T1 - T0, exog=X[T0:T1]).predicted_mean sims = np.asarray(res.simulate(T1 - T0, repetitions=reps, anchor="end", exog=X[T0:T1])).reshape(T1 - T0, -1) return pred, sims pred, sims = impact(y, X, T0) cum = y[T0:].sum() - sims.sum(0) true_cum = (y[T0:] - y[T0:] / 1.10).sum() print(f"Cumulative effect: {y[T0:].sum() - pred.sum():.0f} sign-ups, 95% interval " f"[{np.quantile(cum, .025):.0f}, {np.quantile(cum, .975):.0f}] (true {true_cum:.0f})") ## Cumulative effect: 319 sign-ups, 95% interval [149, 489] (true 473) print(f"Relative effect: {y[T0:].sum() / pred.sum() - 1:+.1%}; " f"simulated paths with effect > 0: {(cum > 0).mean():.1%}") ## Relative effect: +6.5%; simulated paths with effect > 0: 100.0% band = np.quantile(sims, [0.025, 0.975], axis=1) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.9)) ax.plot(t, y, lw=1.2, color="#333", label="Actual") ax.plot(t[T0:], pred, lw=2, ls="--", label="Counterfactual") ax.fill_between(t[T0:], band[0], band[1], alpha=0.2, label="95% interval") ax.axvline(T0, color="#C8102E", lw=1) ax.set_xlabel("Day"); ax.set_ylabel("Sign-ups"); ax.legend(loc="upper left") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 7.2: Actual sign-ups in the treated market versus the models counterfactual and its 95% interval, fitted on the pre-period only. The analysis detects the effect clearly, but the estimate (around 6 to 7%) is well below the true 10%, and the interval only just contains the truth. The treated market has its own slow drift that the controls do not explain. The models interval accounts for that drift on average, but any single analysis can land well off target. This is why one quasi-experimental estimate should be treated as one noisy measurement, and why placebo checks matter. 7.3.2 Placebo in time The most useful robustness check costs one line: pretend the intervention happened earlier, inside the pre-period, and run the same analysis on data where nothing happened. A sound setup should find nothing. pred_p, sims_p = impact(y, X, T0=70, T1=100) cum_p = y[70:100].sum() - sims_p.sum(0) print(f"Placebo (fake start day 70): effect {y[70:100].sum() / pred_p.sum() - 1:+.1%}, 95% interval " f"[{np.quantile(cum_p, .025):.0f}, {np.quantile(cum_p, .975):.0f}] sign-ups") ## Placebo (fake start day 70): effect +0.3%, 95% interval [-118, 146] sign-ups If the placebo finds a significant effect, the model is not tracking the treated series well enough to trust the real result. Run several placebo dates; the share that come out significant is a direct estimate of the methods false positive rate on your data. Choosing control series by trying combinations until the post-period effect looks good. Pick controls on substantive grounds and on pre-period fit only, and fix them before looking at the post-period. 7.4 Synthetic control for a single unit The synthetic control method from Chapter 6 also works for a single treated unit with a pool of untreated donors (other countries, other products). It is more transparent than a structural time series model, because the counterfactual is an explicit weighted average of named donors, and its inference comes from in-space placebos: run the method on each donor as if it had been treated and see whether the real effect stands out. With fewer than about ten donors the placebo distribution is too coarse for a meaningful p-value, and the analysis should be presented as descriptive. 7.5 When there is no control at all Sometimes the only data is the treated series itself: an interrupted time series. You can model trend and seasonality in the pre-period and project forward, but any other change at the same time (a competitor move, a seasonal anomaly, a tracking change) is indistinguishable from the effect. Present the result as weak evidence, show the forecast interval, and look hard at the change log. 7.6 Threats and how to probe them Threat What it looks like Probe Concurrent shock Another change hit the treated unit in the same window Change log, placebo outcomes that should not move Anticipation Behavior changed before the official start (announcements, pre-launch PR) Event-study leads, earlier start date Contaminated controls The intervention also affected the comparison units Check spillover channels; drop suspect controls Unstable relationship Controls tracked well historically but diverged for unrelated reasons Placebo-in-time tests; shorter pre-period Selection into treatment The treated unit was chosen because it was doing badly (or well) Look for regression to the mean in the pre-period Specification search Many models tried, one reported Pre-register controls and windows; report all variants tried 7.7 Checklist Is there a plausible comparison that was not affected by the intervention? For DiD: are event-study pre-period coefficients flat, and are standard errors clustered at the unit level? For staggered rollouts: is a staggered-adoption estimator used instead of plain two-way fixed effects? For CausalImpact: are the controls unaffected, chosen on pre-period grounds only, and fixed before looking? Do placebo-in-time (and, where possible, placebo-in-space) tests come out null? Does the change log show anything else hitting the treated unit in the window? Does the readout name the design as quasi-experimental and list the threats that remain? 7.8 Further reading Googles CausalImpact (R) and tfp-causalimpact (Python), with the many worked examples in the library: SEO changes, offline activities, app downloads versus search interest. Causmos (Google Marketing Solutions). A no-code interface for CausalImpact-style analysis. CausalPy (PyMC Labs). Bayesian synthetic control, DiD, interrupted time series and regression discontinuity in one package. Difference in differences, CausalImpact and synthetic controls (overview article in the library) and Causal Inference: The Mixtape, chapters on DiD and synthetic control. differences, diff-diff and DRDID for modern DiD with staggered adoption. Bootstrap random walks for causal inference on time series (Carlos Agostini). An alternative way to build intervals. Full links are in Appendix A.

Chapter 8 Reading platform lift studies How much to trust an ad platforms own incrementality study, what exactly it measured, and how to turn its result into numbers you can use for budgeting and for correcting the platforms everyday reporting. 8.1 What a lift study is The large ad platforms offer incrementality studies on their own inventory: conversion lift studies that hold out a random share of the target audience from seeing your ads, geo-based variants that hold out regions, and brand lift studies that survey exposed and unexposed users. The details and names change often, so check your platforms current documentation, but the logic is stable. User-level conversion lift is a real randomized experiment. The platform splits the eligible audience at random into a test group, which can be shown your ads, and a holdout, which is not (holdout users see other advertisers ads instead). Conversions in the two groups are compared. Because assignment is random, the comparison is causal in the same sense as any A/B test. That makes a platform lift study much stronger evidence than the platforms attribution reporting, which measures who converted after an ad, not who converted because of one (Chapter 1). It does not make it a complete answer. The randomization is sound; the questions are about what outcome was measured, on whom, under which conditions. 8.2 What exactly was measured Read every lift study against these questions before using its result. Question Why it matters What to look for What is the outcome? The platform can only count conversions it observes Pixel / SDK events versus conversions uploaded from your backend Who was randomized? Results apply to the audience in the test, not to everyone Targeting, exclusions, campaigns included How is the effect scaled? Intent-to-treat versus effect on users who actually saw ads Reach or exposed share; whether results are per eligible or per reached user How big was the holdout? Holdout size drives precision Holdout share, number of conversions in the holdout Which interval is reported? Not every platform reports 95% intervals Confidence or credibility level; Bayesian probabilities of lift Was delivery normal? Campaign changes during the test change what was measured Budget, bidding, creative changes in the test window What window? Long-lag outcomes may fall outside the study Study duration, post-period, conversion window The single most important item is the first. If the study counts only pixel-tracked conversions, it inherits all the signal loss of tracking (Chapter 2): users who convert on another device or without consent are missing from both groups. That usually understates the absolute incremental count while leaving the relative lift roughly intact. Wherever the platform allows it, feed system-of-record conversions into the study (server-side events or offline conversion uploads), so the study measures the outcome you actually care about. 8.3 Worked example: from a study readout to usable numbers A study ran for four weeks with a 10% holdout. The platform reports these totals for the period: import numpy as np import pandas as pd N_t, N_c = 2_000_000, 200_000 # users in test and holdout groups (10% holdout) conv_t, conv_c = 6_300, 560 # conversions observed in each group spend = 150_000 # media spend during the study (EUR) attributed = 2_100 # conversions the platform attributed to the campaign p_t, p_c = conv_t / N_t, conv_c / N_c incr = (p_t - p_c) * N_t # incremental conversions se = np.sqrt(p_t * (1 - p_t) / N_t + p_c * (1 - p_c) / N_c) * N_t lo, hi = incr - 1.96 * se, incr + 1.96 * se out = pd.DataFrame({ "estimate": [p_t / p_c - 1, incr, spend / incr, incr / attributed], "95% low": [lo / (p_c * N_t), lo, spend / hi, lo / attributed], "95% high": [hi / (p_c * N_t), hi, spend / lo, hi / attributed], }, index=["Relative lift", "Incremental conversions", "Incremental CPA (EUR)", "Incrementality factor"]) print(out.round(2).to_string()) ## estimate 95% low 95% high ## Relative lift 0.12 0.04 0.21 ## Incremental conversions 700.00 211.48 1188.52 ## Incremental CPA (EUR) 214.29 126.21 709.29 ## Incrementality factor 0.33 0.10 0.57 print(f"\nPlatform-attributed CPA: {spend / attributed:.0f} EUR") ## ## Platform-attributed CPA: 71 EUR Three things stand out. The relative lift is modest and the interval is wide. A 12.5% lift with an interval from roughly 4% to 21% is typical. The precision is limited by the holdout: only 560 conversions in the control group. The incremental CPA is several times the attributed CPA. The platforms reporting says each conversion costs about 71 EUR. The study says each incremental conversion costs around 214 EUR, and plausibly anywhere from about 125 to over 700. Note that the interval on a cost ratio is skewed: it is computed by inverting the interval on incremental conversions, not by adding and subtracting a margin. The incrementality factor connects the two. About a third of attributed conversions are incremental here, with a wide range. This factor is how a lift study gets used day to day (below). 8.3.1 Intent-to-treat versus reached users The calculation above compares everyone randomized to the test group with everyone in the holdout, including test-group users who never actually saw an ad. That is the intent-to-treat effect, and it is what matters for budgeting, because it answers what did running this campaign do?. Some studies instead report the effect per reached user, comparing exposed users with holdout users who would have been exposed. If only 45% of the test group was reached, and unreached users were unaffected, the effect per reached user is the intent-to-treat effect divided by 0.45. Both numbers are legitimate. Mixing them up overstates or understates the effect by a factor of two or more, so check which one the report gives before comparing studies. 8.4 Sizing the holdout Holdout size trades precision against cost: holdout users are not advertised to, so a bigger holdout means more conversions forgone during the study. The table shows the minimum detectable relative lift (80% power, 5% two-sided) for the audience and baseline rate above, by holdout share. from scipy import stats N, p = 2_200_000, 0.0028 z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) + stats.norm.ppf(0.8) rows = [] for h in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50]: n_c, n_t = N * h, N * (1 - h) mde = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / n_t + 1 / n_c)) / p rows.append({"holdout share": f"{h:.0%}", "holdout conversions": round(n_c * p), "MDE (relative lift)": f"{mde:.1%}"}) print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False)) ## holdout share holdout conversions MDE (relative lift) ## 5% 308 16.4% ## 10% 616 11.9% ## 20% 1232 8.9% ## 30% 1848 7.8% ## 50% 3080 7.1% Going from a 10% to a 20% holdout narrows the MDE noticeably; beyond about 30%, the gains are small and the cost keeps growing. If the expected lift is around 10%, a 10% holdout on this audience is marginal: there is a real chance the study comes back inconclusive. Size the study before launching it, the same way as any test (Chapter 5). 8.5 Using a lift study Incrementality factors. The most practical use is to calibrate everyday platform reporting. Divide incremental conversions by attributed conversions in the same study and apply that factor to the platforms attributed numbers going forward. Platform CPA of 71 EUR and a factor of 0.33 imply an incremental CPA of about 214 EUR, which is the number to compare with other channels and with the value of a conversion. Factors are specific to a platform, campaign type, market and attribution setting, and they drift as targeting and tracking change. Refresh them at least a few times a year and whenever the setup changes materially. MMM calibration. A lift study is also an input for a marketing mix model, as a prior or a calibration target for that channel (Chapter 11), with the caveats above about outcome definition and scaling. Cross-checks. Because the platform designs, runs and reports the study, an occasional independent check with a geo test on backend outcomes (Chapter 6) is good practice for the largest channels. The point is not that platforms report dishonestly; it is that their study measures their tracked outcome under their conditions, and you want to know how well that transfers to your business outcome. Extending a lift result to another market, campaign type or spend level without saying so. A study on prospecting campaigns in one country, at one budget, says little about retargeting in another country at double the budget. When a result is used outside the conditions it was measured in, write that down as an assumption. 8.6 Brand lift studies Brand lift studies survey users in exposed and holdout groups about ad recall, awareness, consideration or intent. They measure stated attitudes, not behavior, and typically have small response samples, so their intervals are wide. They are useful for comparing creative or formats on upper-funnel goals, and as a sanity check that a brand campaign registers at all. They are not evidence of incremental conversions or revenue; for that, use conversion lift or geo tests on business outcomes. 8.7 Checklist Is the outcome the platforms tracked conversion or your system-of-record conversion? Is the result intent-to-treat or per reached user, and does any comparison mix the two? How many conversions were in the holdout, and what MDE did the design have? Which confidence or credibility level is reported? Did budget, bidding or creative change during the study? Is the incrementality factor computed with its interval and stored with the conditions it was measured under (platform, campaign type, market, attribution setting, date)? If the result is applied to another market, campaign or spend level, is that stated as an assumption? 8.8 Further reading Googles Measurement Playbook. Chapter 9 Marketing mix modeling end to end How much each channel contributes to the business outcome and at what return, as the basis for setting the total budget and splitting it across channels. This chapter builds a classical MMM from scratch so that every moving part is visible, and shows where it fails. 9.1 What an MMM is, and what it is not A marketing mix model is a time-series regression of a business outcome (revenue, sign-ups, accounts) on media activity and everything else that drives the outcome: trend, seasonality, prices, promotions, macro conditions. Its output is a decomposition of the outcome into a base and a contribution per channel, from which you get return on spend, response curves and budget scenarios. Its strengths follow from working with aggregates. It needs no user-level tracking, so it is unaffected by signal loss (Chapter 2). It covers every channel, online and offline, in one consistent framework. And it naturally produces the marginal returns that allocation decisions need. Its weaknesses follow from being observational. It learns only from variation in spend that already happened, so a channel whose spend never moved cannot be measured, and a channel whose spend moves with demand will be credited with that demand (Chapter 3). An MMM is a causal claim made with regression, and it is only as good as its assumptions. That is why Chapter 11 is about validating and calibrating it against experiments. 9.2 The building blocks Most MMMs, from a spreadsheet to Googles Meridian, share the same structure: \[ y_t = \text{base}_t + \sum_{c} \beta_c \, f_c\!\left(\text{adstock}_c(x_{c,t})\right) + \varepsilon_t, \] where \(x_{c,t}\) is spend (or impressions) in channel \(c\) in week \(t\), and the base contains intercept, trend, seasonality and controls. Adstock captures carryover: an ad seen this week still affects behavior next week. The simplest form is geometric decay, where a share \(\delta\) of each weeks effect carries into the following week, then \(\delta^2\) into the week after, and so on. TV and brand campaigns typically decay slowly; search and promotional activity decay fast. Delayed adstock forms (for example Weibull-shaped) allow the effect to peak a week or two after the spend. Saturation captures diminishing returns: the tenth million spent in a channel buys less than the first. Common shapes are the Hill function, the negative exponential and the logistic form used here, \(f(x) = (1 - e^{-\lambda x}) / (1 + e^{-\lambda x})\), where larger \(\lambda\) means faster saturation. import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".") import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from pms_sim import geometric_adstock, logistic_saturation pulse = np.r_[1.0, np.zeros(9)] fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 2.5)) for d in [0.1, 0.3, 0.6]: a1.plot(geometric_adstock(pulse, d, l_max=10), marker="o", ms=3, label=f"decay {d}") a1.set_xlabel("Weeks after spend"); a1.set_title("Adstock"); a1.legend() x = np.linspace(0, 2, 100) for lam in [0.5, 1.5, 3.0]: a2.plot(x, logistic_saturation(x, lam), label=f"lambda {lam}") a2.set_xlabel("Spend (scaled)"); a2.set_title("Saturation"); a2.legend() plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 9.1: Left: geometric adstock spreads a single week of spend over the following weeks. Right: logistic saturation for different values of lambda (spend scaled to the channel maximum). Order matters. Applying adstock before saturation (the usual choice) means carryover from past weeks and spend this week saturate together, which suits channels with continuous presence. Saturation before adstock suits bursty channels where each weeks exposure saturates on its own. The base is everything the media does not explain. Getting it right matters more than any media specification, because whatever the base misses, the media terms will absorb. Trend, yearly seasonality (Fourier terms or holiday dummies), promotions, price changes, product launches and known shocks all belong here. 9.3 The data for this part of the book All of Part III uses one simulated dataset so that results can be compared across chapters and against the truth. It has three years of weekly revenue and four channels, built to reproduce the situations real MMMs struggle with: TV runs in flights: six weeks on, twelve weeks off. Plenty of variation, slow decay. Social is planned into the seasonal peak, so its spend is correlated with seasonality. Search spend follows demand, including demand shocks the model cannot observe. Display is always on at an almost constant level. The full simulation is in pms_sim.py: """Simulated weekly marketing data with a known ground truth (Part III).""" import numpy as np import pandas as pd CHANNELS = ["tv", "social", "search", "display"] def geometric_adstock(x, decay, l_max=8): """Carry over a share `decay` of each week's effect into the following weeks.""" w = decay ** np.arange(l_max) return np.convolve(x, w)[: len(x)] def logistic_saturation(x, lam): """Concave response: ~linear for small x, flattening out as x grows.""" return (1 - np.exp(-lam * x)) / (1 + np.exp(-lam * x)) TRUTH = { # per channel: adstock decay, saturation lambda (on spend / channel max), effect size (EUR) "tv": {"decay": 0.60, "lam": 1.5, "beta": 140_000}, "social": {"decay": 0.30, "lam": 2.0, "beta": 90_000}, "search": {"decay": 0.10, "lam": 2.5, "beta": 85_000}, "display": {"decay": 0.30, "lam": 1.0, "beta": 12_000}, } def simulate(seed=2026, n_weeks=156): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) t = np.arange(n_weeks) season = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 52) + 0.4 * np.cos(4 * np.pi * t / 52) shock = np.zeros(n_weeks) # unobserved demand shocks (AR(1)) for i in range(1, n_weeks): shock[i] = 0.7 * shock[i - 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.35) promo = (rng.random(n_weeks) < 0.08).astype(float) spend = pd.DataFrame({ # TV runs in flights: on for some weeks, off for others "tv": np.where((t // 6) % 3 == 0, rng.uniform(40_000, 80_000, n_weeks), 0.0), # Social is planned into the seasonal peak "social": np.clip(30_000 + 9_000 * season + rng.normal(0, 4_000, n_weeks), 5_000, None), # Search spend follows demand, including the unobserved shocks "search": np.clip(20_000 + 4_000 * season + 6_000 * shock + rng.normal(0, 1_500, n_weeks), 3_000, None), # Display is always on at an almost constant level "display": 10_000 + rng.normal(0, 400, n_weeks), }) contrib = pd.DataFrame(index=t) for c in CHANNELS: p = TRUTH[c] x = geometric_adstock(spend[c].to_numpy(), p["decay"]) / spend[c].max() contrib[c] = p["beta"] * logistic_saturation(x, p["lam"]) base = 300_000 + 400 * t + 45_000 * season + 30_000 * shock + 25_000 * promo revenue = base + contrib.sum(1) + rng.normal(0, 9_000, n_weeks) # Category-level search interest: a noisy, observable proxy for demand (not driven by our media) category_demand = 100 + 20 * season + 20 * shock + rng.normal(0, 4, n_weeks) df = pd.DataFrame({"week": pd.date_range("2023-01-02", periods=n_weeks, freq="W-MON"), "revenue": revenue, "promo": promo, "category_demand": category_demand, **spend}) roi = {c: contrib[c].sum() / spend[c].sum() for c in CHANNELS} return df, {"contrib": contrib, "roi": roi, "base": base} from pms_sim import simulate, CHANNELS, TRUTH import pandas as pd df, truth = simulate() summary = df[CHANNELS].agg(["mean", "std"]).T summary["cv"] = summary["std"] / summary["mean"] summary["true ROI"] = pd.Series(truth["roi"]) print(summary.round(2).to_string()) ## mean std cv true ROI ## tv 21345.83 30231.52 1.42 2.43 ## social 30086.51 8504.20 0.28 2.04 ## search 20389.93 4830.19 0.24 2.89 ## display 10017.12 411.24 0.04 0.68 The coefficient of variation (cv) is worth a look before any modeling. Displays spend varies by about 4% around its mean; there is almost nothing to learn its effect from. 9.4 Fitting a classical MMM The model is linear in the effect sizes \(\beta\) once the adstock and saturation parameters are fixed. That suggests a simple two-level fit: an outer search over the eight nonlinear parameters (a decay and a \(\lambda\) per channel), and for each candidate, an inner least-squares fit of the effect sizes and base terms, with media effects constrained to be non-negative. This is the same idea, minus the ridge penalty and multi-objective search, that Metas Robyn uses. from scipy.optimize import lsq_linear, differential_evolution n = len(df); t = np.arange(n) base_terms = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), t / n, np.sin(2*np.pi*t/52), np.cos(2*np.pi*t/52), np.sin(4*np.pi*t/52), np.cos(4*np.pi*t/52), df["promo"]]) X = df[CHANNELS].to_numpy(); x_max = X.max(0); y = df["revenue"].to_numpy() def media_terms(theta): decay, lam = theta[:4], theta[4:] return np.column_stack([logistic_saturation(geometric_adstock(X[:, i], decay[i]) / x_max[i], lam[i]) for i in range(4)]) def inner_fit(theta): M = np.column_stack([media_terms(theta), base_terms]) lower = np.r_[np.zeros(4), np.full(base_terms.shape[1], -np.inf)] # media effects >= 0 return lsq_linear(M, y, bounds=(lower, np.inf)), M bounds = [(0, 0.9)] * 4 + [(0.2, 6)] * 4 opt = differential_evolution(lambda th: (inner_fit(th)[0].fun ** 2).sum(), bounds, seed=1, maxiter=80, tol=1e-8) fit, M = inner_fit(opt.x) contrib_hat = M[:, :4] * fit.x[:4] fitted = M @ fit.x r2 = 1 - ((y - fitted) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum() mape = np.mean(np.abs(y / fitted - 1)) print(f"In-sample R^2 = {r2:.3f}, MAPE = {mape:.1%}") ## In-sample R^2 = 0.979, MAPE = 1.8% res = pd.DataFrame({"true decay": [TRUTH[c]["decay"] for c in CHANNELS], "est. decay": opt.x[:4], "true ROI": [truth["roi"][c] for c in CHANNELS], "est. ROI": contrib_hat.sum(0) / X.sum(0)}, index=CHANNELS) print(res.round(2).to_string()) ## true decay est. decay true ROI est. ROI ## tv 0.6 0.55 2.43 2.28 ## social 0.3 0.10 2.04 1.64 ## search 0.1 0.14 2.89 6.99 ## display 0.3 0.00 0.68 23.18 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.7)) xx = np.arange(4) ax.bar(xx - 0.18, res["true ROI"], 0.36, label="True ROI") ax.bar(xx + 0.18, res["est. ROI"].clip(upper=8), 0.36, label="Estimated ROI (capped at 8)") ax.set_xticks(xx, CHANNELS); ax.set_ylabel("Revenue per EUR"); ax.legend() plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 9.2: Classical MMM: estimated versus true ROI by channel. Excellent fit, wrong answers for two of four channels. 9.5 Reading the result The model fits the data almost perfectly, and two of its four ROIs are badly wrong. Each error has a specific cause, and each cause is common in real data. TV is recovered well. Its spend switches on and off independently of everything else, which is close to a natural experiment. Flighted channels are the easiest to measure. Social is somewhat underestimated. Its spend moves with seasonality, so the seasonal terms and the social coefficient compete to explain the same pattern. The data cannot fully separate them. Search is overstated by more than double. Search spend rises when demand rises, including demand shocks that are not in the model. The search coefficient absorbs those shocks. This is confounding in exactly the sense of Chapter 3, and no amount of fit quality will reveal it. Display is absurd. With almost no variation in spend, display is nearly a constant, so it competes with the intercept. The optimizer happily assigns it a large chunk of base revenue, and the ROI explodes. The model has no information about display at all; it just does not say so. The general lesson is the most important one in this part of the book: goodness of fit is not evidence that the decomposition is right. An MMM can have an R of 0.98 and a MAPE of 2% while attributing base demand to media. Validation has to come from somewhere other than in-sample fit: from priors that encode what is plausible (Chapter 10), and above all from experiments (Chapter 11). Presenting MMM fit statistics as validation. R and MAPE tell you the model reproduces the outcome series; they do not tell you the split between base and media, or between channels, is right. Several very different decompositions usually fit equally well. 9.6 Modeling decisions that matter Decision Options Guidance Outcome Revenue, sign-ups, accounts, first transactions The outcome closest to value that still has enough weekly volume; from the system of record Granularity Weekly or daily; national or by region Weekly is standard. Regional (geo-level) data multiplies the observations and is usually worth the effort Media variable Spend, impressions, GRPs Impressions or GRPs when media prices change over time; spend for budgeting outputs Number of channels Every line item, or grouped Roughly one channel per 15 to 20 weeks of data at most; group small channels Base Trend, seasonality, holidays, promotions, price, macro Include every major non-media driver; missing ones leak into media History 2 to 3 years Long enough to see seasons repeat; short enough that the business is comparable Long-term effects Usually not captured Standard MMMs measure short-term response (weeks); brand-building effects over years need other methods Geo-level data deserves emphasis. A national weekly model has around 150 observations. The same three years by 20 regions have 3,000, and regional variation in spend (from regional TV, from different market sizes, from tests) is often much less confounded than national variation over time. Hierarchical models that share information across regions (Meridian supports this directly) are the main route to more precise MMMs. 9.7 The tool landscape Robyn (Meta, R): ridge regression with evolutionary search over adstock and saturation hyperparameters, producing a set of Pareto-optimal models that trade off fit against how far the decomposition is from current spend shares. Strong on automation; requires judgment in choosing among models. Meridian (Google, Python): a Bayesian MMM with hierarchical geo-level modeling, reach and frequency inputs, and calibration with experiments through ROI priors. It replaces Googles earlier LightweightMMM. PyMC-Marketing (PyMC Labs, Python): a Bayesian MMM with flexible adstock and saturation choices, time-varying effects, lift-test calibration and a budget optimizer. Chapter 10 builds the same kind of model from scratch. Orbit (Uber), Prophet-based approaches, Cassandra and commercial tools (for example Recast) cover other points on the trade-off between flexibility, automation and transparency. Choose a tool for its handling of priors, calibration and uncertainty, not for its fit statistics. 9.8 Checklist Is the outcome from the system of record, and are all major non-media drivers in the base? Does every modeled channel have meaningful spend variation (check the coefficient of variation), and are channels without it grouped or handled with priors? Is there a channel whose spend responds to demand (search, retargeting)? Treat its estimate as an upper bound until tested. Are adstock and saturation choices justified per channel type? Is the ratio of channels to observations reasonable, or is geo-level data available? Is anyone treating R or MAPE as validation? 9.9 Further reading How Facebook Robyn works and Bayesian MMM, MMM checklist, Adstock rates and Seasonality (Recast). Chapter 10 Bayesian MMM in practice The same allocation and budget-level questions as Chapter 9, answered with a model that states its assumptions as priors, reports honest uncertainty, and says plainly when the data cannot tell you something. 10.1 What priors buy you The classical model in Chapter 9 had two failure modes. For display it produced an absurd answer with no warning. For search it produced a confident wrong answer. A Bayesian model fixes the first and makes the second easier to diagnose, but it does not fix the second on its own. Priors help in three concrete ways: They rule out the impossible. Media effects are non-negative, adstock decays are between 0 and 1, and no channel plausibly drives half of revenue on a tenth of the budget. Encoding this stops the model from assigning base revenue to a constant like display. They make the data says nothing visible. When a channels posterior looks just like its prior, the data contributed no information. That is a finding, and it should be reported as one. They are the entry point for experiments. A lift test result can enter the model as a prior or as an extra likelihood term (Chapter 11). This is the main route to fixing confounded channels like search. 10.2 The model The model below is a plain PyMC implementation of the structure from Chapter 9: geometric adstock with an eight-week maximum lag, logistic saturation, and a base with intercept, trend, two pairs of yearly Fourier terms and a promotion dummy. Revenue is scaled by its mean and spend by each channels maximum, so that priors can be stated on comparable scales. Writing it out by hand, rather than calling a library, makes every assumption explicit; the library equivalents come at the end of the chapter. """A compact Bayesian MMM in plain PyMC: geometric adstock + logistic saturation.""" import numpy as np import pymc as pm import pytensor.tensor as pt L_MAX = 8 def lagged(X, l_max=L_MAX): """Array of shape (l_max, n_weeks, n_channels): X shifted by 0..l_max-1 weeks.""" out = np.zeros((l_max,) + X.shape) for l in range(l_max): out[l, l:] = X[: len(X) - l] return out def build_mmm(df, channels, lift=None, controls=()): """df: weekly data with revenue, promo and spend columns. lift: optional dict(channel, start, end, roi, se) from an experiment, used to calibrate. controls: optional extra control columns (standardized inside the model).""" n = len(df) t = np.arange(n) y_scale = df["revenue"].mean() y = df["revenue"].to_numpy() / y_scale X = df[channels].to_numpy() x_scale = X.max(0) Xlag = lagged(X / x_scale) fourier = np.column_stack([f(2 * np.pi * k * t / 52) for k in (1, 2) for f in (np.sin, np.cos)]) spend_share = X.sum(0) / X.sum() coords = {"channel": channels, "week": t, "fourier": ["s1", "c1", "s2", "c2"]} with pm.Model(coords=coords) as model: # Carryover: TV is expected to last longer than digital channels decay = pm.Beta("decay", alpha=np.where(np.array(channels) == "tv", 3.0, 2.0), beta=np.where(np.array(channels) == "tv", 2.0, 3.0), dims="channel") lam = pm.Gamma("lam", alpha=4, beta=2, dims="channel") # Effect sizes, parameterized as each channel's average weekly contribution # (share of mean revenue); prior scale proportional to the channel's share of spend beta = pm.HalfNormal("beta", sigma=0.12 * spend_share / spend_share.max(), dims="channel") weights = decay[None, :] ** np.arange(L_MAX)[:, None] # (lag, channel) adstocked = (Xlag * weights[:, None, :]).sum(axis=0) # (week, channel) sat = (1 - pt.exp(-lam * adstocked)) / (1 + pt.exp(-lam * adstocked)) sat = sat / sat.mean(axis=0) # rescale so that beta = average contribution contrib = pm.Deterministic("contrib", sat * beta, dims=("week", "channel")) # Prior on the overall level (intercept plus average media contribution), not on the # intercept alone: a near-constant channel can then trade off against the intercept # without moving the level, which removes a ridge the sampler otherwise struggles with level = pm.Normal("level", 0.9, 0.3) intercept = pm.Deterministic("intercept", level - beta.sum()) trend = pm.Normal("trend", 0, 0.3) gamma = pm.Normal("gamma", 0, 0.2, dims="fourier") promo = pm.Normal("promo", 0, 0.2) mu = (intercept + trend * t / n + pt.dot(fourier, gamma) + promo * df["promo"].to_numpy() + contrib.sum(axis=1)) if controls: Z = df[list(controls)].to_numpy() Z = (Z - Z.mean(0)) / Z.std(0) delta = pm.Normal("delta", 0, 0.2, shape=len(controls)) mu = mu + pt.dot(Z, delta) sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", 0.1) pm.Normal("y", mu, sigma, observed=y, dims="week") # ROI per channel over the whole period, in EUR revenue per EUR spend pm.Deterministic("roi", contrib.sum(axis=0) * y_scale / X.sum(0), dims="channel") if lift is not None: # experiment-implied ROI over the test window, as an extra likelihood term i = channels.index(lift["channel"]) w = slice(lift["start"], lift["end"]) model_roi = contrib[w, i].sum() * y_scale / X[w, i].sum() pm.Normal("lift_obs", mu=model_roi, sigma=lift["se"], observed=lift["roi"]) return model, {"y_scale": y_scale, "x_scale": x_scale} The priors deserve a word each: Decay: Beta(3, 2) for TV (mean 0.6) and Beta(2, 3) for the digital channels (mean 0.4). This encodes the common finding that TV carries over longer, without forcing it. Saturation: Gamma(4, 2) on \(\lambda\), mean 2, which puts the curves bend somewhere within the observed spend range rather than far outside it. Effect sizes: each channels \(\beta\) is its average weekly contribution as a share of mean revenue (the saturation curve is rescaled to average 1 over the data). Its prior is half-normal with scale proportional to the channels share of spend, a mild belief that bigger budgets go to channels that do more. This mirrors PyMC-Marketings default. It is a choice, not a law; Chapter 11 shows how to check what it does. Level: the prior is placed on the overall level (intercept plus average media contribution) rather than on the intercept, for a reason explained under diagnostics below. 10.3 Prior predictive check Before fitting, simulate from the priors alone and look at what they imply for quantities you can judge: the ROI of each channel and the share of revenue attributed to media. import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".") import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import numpy as np, pandas as pd, pymc as pm from pms_sim import simulate, CHANNELS from pms_mmm import build_mmm df, truth = simulate() model, scales = build_mmm(df, CHANNELS) with model: prior = pm.sample_prior_predictive(1000, random_seed=7) ## Sampling: [beta, decay, gamma, lam, level, promo, sigma, trend, y] roi_prior = prior.prior["roi"].stack(s=("chain", "draw")).values # (channel, draws) media_share = (prior.prior["contrib"].sum(("week", "channel")).values.ravel() / prior.prior_predictive["y"].sum("week").values.ravel()) q = lambda a: np.quantile(a, [0.05, 0.5, 0.95], axis=-1) tbl = pd.DataFrame(q(roi_prior).T, index=CHANNELS, columns=["5%", "median", "95%"]) print("Prior ROI by channel:\n" + tbl.round(2).to_string()) ## Prior ROI by channel: ## 5% median 95% ## tv 0.14 1.45 4.14 ## social 0.15 1.38 4.04 ## search 0.11 1.34 3.80 ## display 0.13 1.45 4.04 lo, med, hi = q(media_share) print(f"\nPrior share of revenue from media: median {med:.0%}, 90% range [{lo:.0%}, {hi:.0%}]") ## ## Prior share of revenue from media: median 29%, 90% range [11%, 89%] Because each channels effect prior scales with its share of spend, the implied ROI prior is similar for every channel, centered a little above 1 with a long right tail: a neutral starting point that does not favor any channel. Total media is expected to drive somewhere between a tenth and most of revenue, with a small chance of more than all of it. This is the second version of the prior, and the first one is worth describing because it shows what the check is for. Initially the effect-size prior had two and a half times the scale used here. It looked reasonable written down, but its prior predictive check implied a median media share of about 72% of revenue and a 90% range reaching over 200%: a belief, before seeing any data, that media plausibly drives twice the business. Tightening the scale brought the implied quantities back into a defensible range. Nothing about the data was used to make that change; it was a correction of the prior to match what we actually believe. That is the purpose of the prior predictive check, and it is why the check comes before fitting. 10.4 Fitting and diagnostics Fitting is a single call. Three years of weekly data with four channels samples in a few minutes on a laptop. with model: idata = pm.sample(1000, tune=1500, chains=4, target_accept=0.95, random_seed=3) pm.sample_posterior_predictive(idata, extend_inferencedata=True, random_seed=3) Before reading any result, check that the sampler worked. Three checks cover most problems: no (or very few) divergent transitions, R-hat close to 1 for every parameter (chains agree), and an effective sample size in the hundreds or more (enough independent draws). post = idata.posterior n_div = int(idata.sample_stats["diverging"].sum()) rhat = az.rhat(post, var_names=["decay", "lam", "beta", "level", "sigma"]) ess = az.ess(post, var_names=["decay", "lam", "beta", "level", "sigma"]) max_rhat = max(float(rhat[v].max()) for v in rhat.data_vars) min_ess = min(float(ess[v].min()) for v in ess.data_vars) print(f"Divergences: {n_div}; max R-hat: {max_rhat:.3f}; min ESS: {min_ess:.0f}") ## Divergences: 0; max R-hat: 1.004; min ESS: 2702 Getting to a clean run took one change worth describing, because it is typical. The first version of this model put the prior on the intercept and produced a few dozen divergent transitions. Comparing divergent draws with the rest showed where they came from: they clustered where displays effect was large and the intercept small. Display spend is nearly constant, so the data identifies only the sum of the intercept and displays contribution; the sampler was exploring a long, narrow ridge between them, bounded by displays effect being non-negative. Placing the prior on the overall level and deriving the intercept from it (intercept = level - sum(beta)) turns that ridge into a direction along which the level does not move, and the divergences disappear. When divergences appear, the fix is almost always a reparameterization or a better prior, not a higher target_accept. Then check that the model reproduces the data it was fitted on. The posterior predictive check overlays the observed series on the models predictive interval. Like R, this is a necessary condition, not evidence that the decomposition is right. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ppc = idata.posterior_predictive["y"].stack(s=("chain", "draw")).values * scales["y_scale"] band = np.quantile(ppc, [0.05, 0.95], axis=1) cover = np.mean((df["revenue"] >= band[0]) & (df["revenue"] <= band[1])) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8)) ax.fill_between(df["week"], band[0] / 1e3, band[1] / 1e3, alpha=0.25, label="90% predictive interval") ax.plot(df["week"], df["revenue"] / 1e3, lw=1, color="#333", label="Observed") ax.set_ylabel("Revenue (EUR k)"); ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() Figure 10.1: Posterior predictive check: observed weekly revenue against the models 90% predictive interval. print(f"Share of weeks inside the 90% interval: {cover:.0%}") ## Share of weeks inside the 90% interval: 92% 10.5 Results: what the posterior says roi_post = post["roi"].stack(s=("chain", "draw")).values classical = {"tv": 2.28, "social": 1.64, "search": 6.99, "display": 23.18} # from Chapter 9 res = pd.DataFrame({ "true": [truth["roi"][c] for c in CHANNELS], "classical": [classical[c] for c in CHANNELS], "posterior median": np.median(roi_post, 1), "90% low": np.quantile(roi_post, 0.05, 1), "90% high": np.quantile(roi_post, 0.95, 1), "prior 90% width": np.diff(np.quantile(roi_prior, [0.05, 0.95], 1), axis=0)[0], "posterior 90% width": np.diff(np.quantile(roi_post, [0.05, 0.95], 1), axis=0)[0], }, index=CHANNELS) print(res.round(2).to_string()) ## true classical posterior median 90% low 90% high prior 90% width posterior 90% width ## tv 2.43 2.28 2.27 2.18 2.36 4.00 0.18 ## social 2.04 1.64 1.52 0.76 2.60 3.89 1.83 ## search 2.89 6.99 6.54 5.78 7.49 3.69 1.71 ## display 0.68 23.18 1.04 0.08 3.39 3.91 3.31 nums = {col: {c: float(v) for c, v in res[col].items()} for col in res.columns} # for inline text fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.9)) yy = np.arange(4)[::-1] ax.errorbar(res["posterior median"], yy, xerr=[res["posterior median"] - res["90% low"], res["90% high"] - res["posterior median"]], fmt="o", capsize=4, label="Posterior (90%)") ax.scatter(res["true"], yy, marker="x", s=60, color="#C8102E", zorder=3, label="Truth") ax.set_yticks(yy, CHANNELS); ax.set_xlabel("ROI (revenue per EUR)"); ax.legend(loc="lower right") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 10.2: Posterior ROI by channel (median and 90% interval) against the truth. Displays interval is mostly prior; searchs is precise and wrong. Compare this with the classical fit, channel by channel. TV is close to the truth, and its interval is narrow (2.18 to 2.36). Look closely, though: the true value of 2.43 sits just above it. Even the best-identified channel absorbs a little bias from what the model gets wrong elsewhere, and a 90% interval is a statement about uncertainty given the model, not a guarantee. Display is no longer absurd. Its posterior median is 1.04 against a true 0.68, but look at the widths: its posterior interval is nearly as wide as its prior interval. The data has told the model almost nothing about display, and the posterior is mostly the prior speaking. The correct readout is we cannot measure display with this data, and the correct action is an experiment, not a budget decision based on this number. Search is still badly overstated, with a median of 6.54 against a true 2.89, and its interval is narrow. This is the dangerous case. Priors regularize; they do not remove confounding. The model sees search spend rising when revenue rises and has no way to know that both are driven by demand shocks it cannot observe. A Bayesian model is just as fooled as a classical one, only with tighter intervals around the wrong answer. Social sits between the two: its estimate competes with the seasonal terms, and the interval reflects that. The lesson for practice: read the posterior for each channel against its prior. A narrow posterior far from the prior means the data is informative, which is good news only if the channels spend is not confounded with demand. A posterior that looks like the prior means the data is uninformative. Both cases point to the same next step for the channels that matter: an experiment, which is where Chapter 11 picks up. Taking a narrow posterior interval as proof of a well-measured effect. Interval width reflects the information in the data given the model; it says nothing about bias from a missing confounder. Search spend that follows demand will produce a tight, wrong interval in any MMM, Bayesian or not. 10.6 The same model with PyMC-Marketing Libraries wrap this structure with sensible defaults, plotting and optimization. With PyMC-Marketing (version 1.x at the time of writing), the equivalent model is set up roughly as follows; check the current documentation, because the API evolves. from pymc_marketing.mmm import MMM, GeometricAdstock, LogisticSaturation mmm = MMM( date_column="week", channel_columns=["tv", "social", "search", "display"], control_columns=["promo"], adstock=GeometricAdstock(l_max=8), saturation=LogisticSaturation(), yearly_seasonality=2, ) X = df.drop(columns="revenue") mmm.fit(X, df["revenue"], target_accept=0.95, random_seed=3) # Calibration with a lift test (Chapter 11) and budget optimization (Chapter 12) # are built in: see mmm.add_lift_test_measurements() and the budget optimizer. Googles Meridian takes a similar approach with a different emphasis: it is built for geo-level hierarchical data, models reach and frequency directly, and is typically parameterized with priors on ROI rather than on raw coefficients, which makes it natural to plug in experiment results as ROI priors. 10.7 Checklist Is every prior written down with a reason, and does the prior predictive check imply plausible ROIs and media shares? Were divergences, R-hat and effective sample sizes checked before reading results? Does the posterior predictive check cover the data at roughly the nominal rate? For each channel, how does the posterior compare with the prior? Which channels are data-driven and which are prior-driven? Which channels spend responds to demand? Are their estimates flagged as likely upward-biased until tested? 10.8 Further reading PyMC-Marketing documentation, especially the MMM example notebook and Convenient Bayesian MMM with PyMC-Marketing (Towards Data Science); the PyMC tutorial on YouTube (Business Science). Chapter 11 Validating and calibrating MMM Whether an MMMs channel estimates can be trusted for budget decisions, which checks actually catch the errors that matter, and how to use experiments to correct the model where it is wrong. 11.1 What validation has to catch Chapters 9 and 10 showed two kinds of error in the same dataset. Display was unidentified: the data said nothing about it, and the classical model produced nonsense while the Bayesian one returned its prior. Search was confounded: its spend follows demand, and both models credited it with that demand, precisely and wrongly. A validation procedure is only useful if it can catch both. The table below lists the common checks and what each can and cannot detect. Check Catches Does not catch In-sample fit (R, MAPE, posterior predictive) Gross misspecification Wrong decomposition; confounding Out-of-sample forecast Overfitting; unstable base Wrong decomposition; confounding Stability across refits and windows Unidentified channels (estimates jump) Stable confounding Prior sensitivity Prior-driven channels Confounding Parameter recovery on simulated data Method that cannot recover truth even in principle Problems specific to your real data Business sense checks (base share, ROI ranges) Absurd results Plausible but wrong results Agreement with experiments Confounding and bias of all kinds Only covers channels and periods that were tested Only the last row catches confounding. Everything else is useful, but none of it can tell you that a precise, stable, plausible, well-fitting estimate is biased. 11.2 Out-of-sample forecasts and stability A common first check is to refit the model on a shorter history and forecast the following quarter. We do this for the classical model from Chapter 9, at four cut-off points, and record both the forecast error and each channels estimated ROI. import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".") import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import numpy as np, pandas as pd from pms_sim import simulate, CHANNELS from pms_classical import fit_classical df, truth = simulate() X, y, promo = df[CHANNELS].to_numpy(), df["revenue"].to_numpy(), df["promo"].to_numpy() rows = [] for end in [104, 117, 130, 143]: _, _, predict = fit_classical(X[:end], y[:end], promo[:end]) yhat, contrib = predict(X[:end + 13], promo[:end + 13]) rows.append({"fit on weeks": f"1-{end}", "next-13-week MAPE": f"{np.mean(np.abs(y[end:end+13] / yhat[end:end+13] - 1)):.1%}", **{c: round(contrib[:end, i].sum() / X[:end, i].sum(), 2) for i, c in enumerate(CHANNELS)}}) out = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("fit on weeks") out.loc["truth"] = ["", *[round(truth["roi"][c], 2) for c in CHANNELS]] print(out.to_string()) ## next-13-week MAPE tv social search display ## fit on weeks ## 1-104 2.0% 2.20 1.44 6.58 29.61 ## 1-117 1.5% 2.25 1.45 6.88 41.00 ## 1-130 1.9% 2.21 1.32 7.39 24.86 ## 1-143 1.4% 2.26 1.51 7.35 16.36 ## truth 2.43 2.04 2.89 0.68 The out-of-sample forecasts are excellent in every window, around 2% error. On that basis alone, the model would pass most validation reviews. The stability check is more revealing: displays ROI jumps around wildly between windows, which correctly flags it as unidentified. Search, however, is perfectly stable at more than twice its true value. Stability catches unidentified channels; it does not catch confounded ones, because confounding is a stable feature of the data. 11.3 Calibrating with experiments Suppose a geo test on search ran for 12 weeks (weeks 121 to 132) and measured an ROI of 2.83 with a standard error of 0.4 over that window, on backend revenue. That is exactly the kind of evidence that can correct a confounded channel. There are two common ways to bring it into a Bayesian MMM: As a prior on the channels ROI. Simple, and the approach Meridian is built around. The weakness is that the experiment measured the ROI in one window at one spend level, while the prior applies to the whole period. As an extra likelihood term. The model computes the ROI it implies for the test window and spend level, and that implied value is compared with the measurement. This is how PyMC-Marketings lift-test calibration works, and it is what build_mmm does when given a lift argument (the last block of the model code in Chapter 10). lift = {"channel": "search", "start": 120, "end": 132, "roi": 2.83, "se": 0.4} model, _ = build_mmm(df, CHANNELS, lift=lift) A second, independent fix targets the cause rather than the symptom. Search is confounded because its spend responds to demand the model cannot see. If an observable proxy for that demand exists, adding it as a control blocks the confounding path (Chapter 3). Here we use a category-level demand index, such as category search interest from a trends tool. The choice of proxy matters: branded search volume would be a bad control, because our own media drive it, which makes it a mediator rather than a confounder. We fitted four versions of the model: the base model, the model calibrated with the geo test, the model with the demand proxy, and the model with both. import arviz as az names = {"base": "Base", "calibrated": "Geo test cal.", "proxy": "Demand proxy", "proxy_calibrated": "Proxy + cal."} roi = {k: az.from_netcdf(f"_cache/mmm_{k}.nc").posterior["roi"].stack(s=("chain", "draw")).values for k in names} tab = pd.DataFrame({names[k]: [f"{np.median(r[i]):.2f} [{np.quantile(r[i], .05):.2f}, {np.quantile(r[i], .95):.2f}]" for i in range(4)] for k, r in roi.items()}, index=CHANNELS) tab["truth"] = [round(truth["roi"][c], 2) for c in CHANNELS] print("ROI, posterior median [90% interval]:\n" + tab.to_string()) ## ROI, posterior median [90% interval]: ## Base Geo test cal. Demand proxy Proxy + cal. truth ## tv 2.27 [2.18, 2.36] 2.24 [2.15, 2.34] 2.30 [2.23, 2.37] 2.30 [2.23, 2.38] 2.43 ## social 1.52 [0.76, 2.60] 1.78 [0.88, 3.00] 1.68 [0.99, 2.60] 1.71 [1.01, 2.66] 2.04 ## search 6.54 [5.78, 7.49] 4.74 [4.28, 5.21] 3.36 [2.20, 4.67] 3.09 [2.47, 3.73] 2.89 ## display 1.04 [0.08, 3.39] 1.23 [0.10, 3.73] 1.07 [0.11, 3.35] 1.07 [0.09, 3.26] 0.68 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt i = CHANNELS.index("search") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6)) yy = np.arange(4)[::-1] for y_, (k, r) in zip(yy, roi.items()): lo, med, hi = np.quantile(r[i], [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]) ax.errorbar(med, y_, xerr=[[med - lo], [hi - med]], fmt="o", capsize=4, color="#1F4E79") ax.axvline(truth["roi"]["search"], ls="--", color="#C8102E", label="True search ROI") ax.set_yticks(yy, list(names.values())); ax.set_xlabel("Search ROI"); ax.legend(loc="lower right") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 11.1: Search ROI under four model specifications (median and 90% interval) against the truth (dashed). 11.4 What calibration did and did not do Calibration alone helped, but not enough. The geo test pulled search from about 6.5 to under 5, a large correction, yet the interval still excludes the truth. The reason is instructive. The experiment constrains what the model says about weeks 121 to 132. In the other 144 weeks, nothing has changed: search spend still moves with unobserved demand, and the model can still credit it with that demand. It reconciles the two by fitting the test window as well as it can while keeping search high elsewhere. A single short experiment cannot overrule three years of confounded variation. The demand proxy addressed the cause. With a control for category demand, the search estimate falls to the right neighborhood and the interval widens to an honest width that contains the truth. Blocking the confounding path is more powerful than correcting the estimate after the fact. Both together were best. The proxy removes most of the bias, and the experiment then sharpens the estimate. The result is close to the truth with a usefully narrow interval. Display remains unmeasured in every version. No amount of modeling fixes a channel with no variation. It needs its own experiment. Two practical conclusions follow. First, treat calibration as part of model building, not as a patch: when an experiment and the model disagree strongly, ask why the model is wrong, and fix the specification if you can, rather than only adding the experiment as a constraint. Second, one experiment per channel is a starting point. Repeated tests across seasons and spend levels constrain the model in more places and leave it less room to hide bias outside the test windows. Calibrating an MMM to platform-attributed results, or to lift studies that measured a different outcome. Calibration transfers whatever the experiment measured into the model. If the experiment measured pixel conversions in another market, the model is now calibrated to that. 11.5 Calibrating well Match the conditions. Use the experiments window, spend level, market and outcome definition. A likelihood term on the test window does this naturally; an ROI prior on the whole period does not. Inflate uncertainty for transport. If conditions differ (different season, spend level or market), widen the experiments standard error to reflect the gap, as in the bias allowances of Chapter 14. Prefer go-dark and scale-back tests for the channels the model is least sure about, and heavy-up tests where the decision is about growth, so that the calibration covers the part of the response curve the decision depends on. Keep a log of every experiment used for calibration, with its conditions, so that the models evidence base is auditable. 11.6 Other validation worth doing Parameter recovery on simulated data. Everything in this part of the book is an example of it: simulate data with known truth that resembles your real situation (spend patterns, correlations, noise) and check whether the model recovers the truth. If it cannot recover known effects in simulation, it will not recover unknown ones in reality. Metas siMMMulator automates this. Prior sensitivity. Refit with meaningfully different reasonable priors. Channels whose estimates move a lot are prior-driven, which should be stated in any readout. Business sense checks. Base share of the outcome, ROIs against benchmarks from your own past experiments, and the implied effect of switching a channel off should all be plausible to someone who knows the business. Implausible results usually mean a missing control. 11.7 Checklist Has the model been refit on several windows, and are unstable channels flagged as unidentified? Is every channels estimate compared with an experiment where one exists? For channels whose spend responds to demand, is there a demand proxy that is a confounder (category level) rather than a mediator (brand level)? Are experiments used for calibration matched to the models outcome, market and spend level, with uncertainty inflated where they are not? Has parameter recovery been checked on data simulated to resemble the real situation? Chapter 12 Response curves and budget optimization How much to spend in total and how to split it across channels, based on marginal returns rather than averages, with an honest view of how much a recommended reallocation is likely to gain and how much it could lose. 12.1 Average returns do not set budgets A channels ROI from an MMM is an average over everything spent in it. Budget decisions are about the next euro, or the last one, and with diminishing returns those are worth less than the average. The response curve shows expected revenue as a function of spend; its slope is the marginal ROI. Two rules follow, and they are worth stating plainly because they are so often ignored: Move money from channels with low marginal ROI to channels with high marginal ROI, until marginal returns are equal or a constraint binds. This is the logic behind classic results such as the Dorfman-Steiner condition on optimal advertising. Grow the total budget while the marginal return beats the cost of capital, measured on profit, not revenue. If gross margin is 60%, a euro of spend has to bring back about 1.67 euros of revenue at the margin just to break even. A channel with an excellent average ROI can be a poor place for the next euro if it is near saturation, and a channel with a mediocre average can be the best place for it if it is far from saturation. 12.2 Response curves from the posterior Each posterior draw of the Bayesian MMM defines one response curve per channel. We use the best specification from Chapter 11, the model that includes the category demand proxy and is calibrated with the search geo test, and compute the steady-state weekly revenue that a constant weekly spend level would produce. (For a flighted channel such as TV, a steady weekly level is an approximation; budget tools usually also model flighting patterns.) import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".") import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import numpy as np, pandas as pd, arviz as az import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from pms_sim import simulate, CHANNELS, TRUTH, logistic_saturation from pms_mmm import lagged, L_MAX df, truth = simulate() X = df[CHANNELS].to_numpy(); x_scale = X.max(0); y_scale = df["revenue"].mean() Xlag = lagged(X / x_scale) current = X.mean(0) # average weekly spend per channel rng = np.random.default_rng(0) def load_draws(name, k=500): post = az.from_netcdf(f"_cache/mmm_{name}.nc").posterior get = lambda v: post[v].stack(s=("chain", "draw")).values # (channel, draws) idx = rng.choice(get("beta").shape[1], k, replace=False) d = {v: get(v)[:, idx] for v in ["decay", "lam", "beta"]} w = d["decay"][None] ** np.arange(L_MAX)[:, None, None] # (lag, channel, draw) adst = np.einsum("lwc,lcs->wcs", Xlag, w) d["norm"] = logistic_saturation(adst, d["lam"][None]).mean(0) # rescaling used in the model d["carry"] = w.sum(0) # steady-state adstock multiplier return d def weekly_revenue(spend, d): """Expected weekly revenue per channel (channel, draw) at constant weekly spend levels.""" a = (np.asarray(spend)[:, None] / x_scale[:, None]) * d["carry"] return d["beta"] * y_scale * logistic_saturation(a, d["lam"]) / d["norm"] def true_weekly_revenue(spend): out = [] for i, c in enumerate(CHANNELS): p = TRUTH[c] a = spend[i] / x_scale[i] * (p["decay"] ** np.arange(L_MAX)).sum() out.append(p["beta"] * logistic_saturation(a, p["lam"])) return np.array(out) draws = {name: load_draws(name) for name in ["base", "calibrated", "proxy_calibrated"]} d = draws["proxy_calibrated"] fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(8, 4.4)) for i, (c, ax) in enumerate(zip(CHANNELS, axes.ravel())): grid = np.linspace(0, 2.0 * current[i], 60) curves = np.array([weekly_revenue(np.where(np.arange(4) == i, g, 0.0), d)[i] for g in grid]) lo, med, hi = np.quantile(curves, [0.05, 0.5, 0.95], axis=1) ax.fill_between(grid / 1e3, lo / 1e3, hi / 1e3, alpha=0.2) ax.plot(grid / 1e3, med / 1e3, lw=2, label="Model") ax.plot(grid / 1e3, [true_weekly_revenue(np.where(np.arange(4) == i, g, 0.0))[i] / 1e3 for g in grid], ls="--", color="#C8102E", label="Truth") ax.axvline(current[i] / 1e3, ls=":", color="#6B6B6B") ax.set_title(c); ax.set_xlabel("Weekly spend (EUR k)"); ax.set_ylabel("Revenue (EUR k)") axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 12.1: Weekly response curves from the calibrated model with demand proxy (median and 90% band), the true curves (dashed), and current average spend (dotted). 12.3 Marginal ROI at current spend def marginal_roi(spend, d, step=0.01): up = weekly_revenue(spend * (1 + step), d) return (up - weekly_revenue(spend, d)) / (spend[:, None] * step) rows = {} for name, d in draws.items(): m = marginal_roi(current, d) rows[name] = [f"{np.median(m[i]):.2f} [{np.quantile(m[i], .05):.2f}, {np.quantile(m[i], .95):.2f}]" for i in range(4)] true_m = (true_weekly_revenue(current * 1.01) - true_weekly_revenue(current)) / (current * 0.01) tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=CHANNELS) tbl["truth"] = true_m.round(2) print("Marginal ROI at current spend, median [90% interval]:\n" + tbl.to_string()) ## Marginal ROI at current spend, median [90% interval]: ## base calibrated proxy_calibrated truth ## tv 2.44 [2.36, 2.53] 2.41 [2.32, 2.50] 2.48 [2.40, 2.54] 2.58 ## social 0.83 [0.41, 1.25] 0.93 [0.48, 1.48] 0.90 [0.54, 1.30] 1.31 ## search 5.97 [5.44, 6.47] 4.62 [4.11, 5.04] 2.11 [1.41, 2.71] 1.82 ## display 0.24 [0.00, 1.69] 0.28 [0.00, 2.11] 0.24 [0.00, 1.44] 0.52 Compare these with the average ROIs in Chapter 10. For social, search and display, the marginal return is well below the average: the next euro buys much less than the typical one. Search is the starkest case. Its true marginal ROI is under 2 against an average near 3, and the uncalibrated model puts it near 6. Only the model that both controls for demand and is calibrated with the geo test gets close. TV is the exception, and an instructive one: its marginal ROI at a steady average spend level is slightly above its average ROI. TV actually ran in heavy flights, which push each flight further up the saturation curve than the same budget spread evenly would. The response curve answers what if we spent this much every week, which is a different plan from the one that generated the data. Curves for flighted channels need to be read with the flighting pattern in mind. 12.4 Optimizing the allocation With the total weekly budget held fixed, we search for the allocation that maximizes expected revenue, averaging over posterior draws, with each channel kept between 50% and 150% of its current level. The bounds are not a technicality: outside the range of spend the model has seen, the curves are extrapolations driven by the functional form and the priors, and an unconstrained optimizer will happily exploit that. from scipy.optimize import minimize budget = current.sum() def optimize(d): # Optimize over multipliers of current spend: well-scaled for the optimizer obj = lambda m: -weekly_revenue(m * current, d).sum(0).mean() / y_scale r = minimize(obj, np.ones(4), method="SLSQP", bounds=[(0.5, 1.5)] * 4, constraints={"type": "eq", "fun": lambda m: (m * current).sum() / budget - 1}) return r.x * current results = {} for name, d in draws.items(): alloc = optimize(d) model_gain = weekly_revenue(alloc, d).sum(0) - weekly_revenue(current, d).sum(0) # per draw true_gain = true_weekly_revenue(alloc).sum() - true_weekly_revenue(current).sum() results[name] = {**{c: alloc[i] / current[i] - 1 for i, c in enumerate(CHANNELS)}, "forecast gain": model_gain.mean(), "P(gain>0)": (model_gain > 0).mean(), "true gain": true_gain} out = pd.DataFrame(results).T fmt = out.copy() for c in CHANNELS: fmt[c] = out[c].map("{:+.0%}".format) for c in ["forecast gain", "true gain"]: fmt[c] = out[c].map("{:,.0f}".format) fmt["P(gain>0)"] = out["P(gain>0)"].map("{:.0%}".format) print("Change in weekly spend by channel; weekly revenue gain (EUR):\n" + fmt.to_string()) ## Change in weekly spend by channel; weekly revenue gain (EUR): ## tv social search display forecast gain P(gain>0) true gain ## base +46% -50% +50% -50% 55,217 100% 6,826 ## calibrated +40% -46% +50% -50% 40,720 100% 6,945 ## proxy_calibrated +50% -37% +27% -50% 15,583 99% 11,371 gains = {m: {k: float(out.loc[m, k]) for k in ["forecast gain", "true gain"]} for m in out.index} This table is the core lesson of the chapter. Each row is the recommendation a model would make with the same budget, scored twice: by the models own forecast, and by what the reallocation would truly deliver. The uncalibrated model believes search has a high marginal return, so it pushes search to its upper bound. It forecasts a weekly gain of 55,217 EUR and is certain the gain is positive. Following its advice would truly gain 6,826 EUR a week. That is still a gain, mostly because moving money from social and display into TV happens to be right, but it is a fraction of what was promised. The model calibrated with the geo test alone still overstates search, still pushes it to the bound, and still overpromises: a forecast of 40,720 EUR against a true 6,945 EUR. The model that controls for demand and is calibrated moves less money into search and more into TV. It forecasts 15,583 EUR and truly delivers 11,371 EUR: the largest real gain of the three, and the only forecast close to reality. An optimizer is an amplifier. It takes whatever the model believes most confidently and acts on it at the boundary of what it is allowed to do. If that belief is a confounded coefficient, the optimizer turns a measurement error into a budget error. This is why optimization should come last, after calibration, and why the constraints should be tight until the curves have been tested. Running a budget optimizer on an uncalibrated MMM and presenting the result as a plan. The channels most likely to be overstated (those whose spend follows demand) are exactly the ones an optimizer will push hardest. 12.5 Setting the total budget The same machinery answers the level question: increase the total budget in steps, re-optimize the split at each step, and track the marginal return of the last euro. Stop where it falls below the break-even threshold on profit (1.67 at a 60% margin in the example above), or below the return available from other uses of the money. Report the answer as a range, because the marginal returns uncertainty grows quickly as spend moves away from historical levels. 12.6 Turning a recommendation into a test The most defensible way to act on an optimizer is to treat its output as a hypothesis. Move part of the way toward the recommended allocation, in a way that can be measured: a heavy-up in a subset of regions for the channel the model wants to grow, a scale-back in regions for the channel it wants to cut (Chapter 6). The result either confirms the curve, in which case you move further, or corrects it, in which case the model is recalibrated. Over a few cycles this converges on an allocation that rests on measured marginal returns rather than on functional-form assumptions. 12.7 Checklist Is the decision based on marginal ROI at current spend, not average ROI? Is the break-even threshold set on profit (margin-adjusted), not revenue? Are the curves from a calibrated model, and are channels with confounded or prior-dominated estimates flagged? Are optimizer bounds kept within the historically observed spend range? Is the expected gain reported with its uncertainty and the probability of a loss? Is the recommendation implemented as a measurable step (heavy-up or scale-back test) rather than all at once? 12.8 Further reading Diminishing returns and saturation, Diminishing returns model and Marginal CPA resources in the library; What am I willing to pay per click? and Bid simulator and marginal CPA (VexPower) for the paid-search version of the same logic.
