Chapter 20 Forecasting and anomaly detection What to expect next week, month and quarter (for targets, pacing and budgets), and how to tell, day by day, whether a movement in a key metric is a real problem or ordinary noise. 20.1 Two jobs for the same model Forecasting turns up in marketing science in two roles. Planning forecasts set targets and budgets: how many sign-ups to expect next quarter, how much spend that will take, whether the plan is on pace. Monitoring uses a forecast as a moving baseline: if todays number is far outside what the model expected for a day like today, something may be wrong. The same model serves both, and the quality bar is the same: honest uncertainty and an evaluation on data the model has not seen. A third role, the counterfactual forecast that estimates what would have happened without an intervention, was covered in Chapter 7. The difference is the question asked, not the method. 20.2 The data Three years of daily sign-ups with a gentle upward trend, a strong weekly pattern (weekends are quiet), a yearly cycle, and holiday periods where activity drops. import numpy as np, pandas as pd, warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import statsmodels.api as sm from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel import matplotlib.pyplot as plt rng = np.random.default_rng(20) dates = pd.date_range("2023-01-01", "2025-12-31", freq="D") t = np.arange(len(dates)) def is_holiday(idx): return (((idx.month == 12) & (idx.day >= 24)) | ((idx.month == 1) & (idx.day <= 1)) | ((idx.month == 8) & idx.day.isin(range(10, 20)))) weekday_effect = np.array([0.05, 0.08, 0.06, 0.04, 0.0, -0.45, -0.55]) log_mu = (np.log(400) + 0.0004 * t + weekday_effect[dates.dayofweek] + 0.12 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * dates.dayofyear / 365.25) - 0.35 * is_holiday(dates)) signups = pd.Series(rng.negative_binomial(150, 150 / (150 + np.exp(log_mu))).astype(float), index=dates) 20.3 Three forecasters and a fair test We compare three approaches, from simplest to most structured: Seasonal naive: next week looks like last week. Surprisingly hard to beat, and the right baseline for any forecast. Exponential smoothing (ETS) with a damped trend and weekly seasonality, fitted on log sign-ups. Regression on log sign-ups with a trend, day-of-week effects, yearly Fourier terms and a holiday indicator. The test is a rolling-origin backtest: at a series of dates through the final year, fit each model on everything before that date and forecast the next 28 days. Accuracy is measured with MASE (mean absolute error scaled by the error of a seasonal naive forecast in training; below 1 means better than naive) and the coverage of the 90% prediction interval (it should contain about 90% of actual days). def design(idx): X = pd.DataFrame({"trend": (idx - dates[0]).days / 365}, index=idx) for k in range(1, 7): X[f"dow{k}"] = (idx.dayofweek == k).astype(float) for k in (1, 2, 3): X[f"s{k}"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * idx.dayofyear / 365.25) X[f"c{k}"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * idx.dayofyear / 365.25) X["holiday"] = is_holiday(idx).astype(float) return sm.add_constant(X, has_constant="add") H = 28 rows = [] for origin in pd.date_range("2025-01-05", "2025-11-30", freq="28D"): train = signups[:origin - pd.Timedelta(days=1)] test = signups[origin:origin + pd.Timedelta(days=H - 1)] scale = np.mean(np.abs(train.values[7:] - train.values[:-7])) naive = np.tile(train.values[-7:], H // 7 + 1)[:H] ets = ETSModel(np.log1p(train[-730:]).asfreq("D"), error="add", trend="add", damped_trend=True, seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=7).fit(disp=False) e = ets.get_prediction(start=test.index[0], end=test.index[-1]).summary_frame(alpha=0.1) reg = sm.OLS(np.log1p(train), design(train.index)).fit() r = reg.get_prediction(design(test.index)).summary_frame(alpha=0.1) for name, f, lo, hi in [("Seasonal naive", naive, None, None), ("ETS", np.expm1(e["mean"]), np.expm1(e["pi_lower"]), np.expm1(e["pi_upper"])), ("Regression", np.expm1(r["mean"]), np.expm1(r["obs_ci_lower"]), np.expm1(r["obs_ci_upper"]))]: f = np.asarray(f) rows.append({"model": name, "MASE": np.mean(np.abs(test.values - f)) / scale, "MAPE": np.mean(np.abs(test.values - f) / test.values), "90% interval coverage": np.nan if lo is None else np.mean((test.values >= np.asarray(lo)) & (test.values <= np.asarray(hi)))}) bt = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("model").mean() print(bt.round(2).to_string(na_rep="n/a")) ## MASE MAPE 90% interval coverage ## model ## ETS 1.03 0.11 0.92 ## Regression 0.74 0.08 0.92 ## Seasonal naive 1.34 0.14 n/a The regression wins here, mainly because it knows about holidays and the yearly cycle, which ETS (with only weekly seasonality) and the naive forecast do not. Both model-based forecasters produce intervals with close to nominal coverage. In real data the ranking varies, which is the point of backtesting: the right model is the one that wins on your history, at your forecast horizon, not the one that sounds most sophisticated. Evaluating a forecast on the data it was fitted on, or on a single holdout period. In-sample fit rewards overfitting, and one period can be unusually easy or hard. Use a rolling-origin backtest at the horizon you actually need. 20.4 Anomaly detection: is todays number a problem? Monitoring dashboards often flag a metric when it moves more than some percentage from yesterday or from last week. On data with strong weekly patterns, that rule fires every Saturday and Monday, and on holidays, and people learn to ignore it. A better rule compares each day with what a forecast expected for that day, and flags residuals that are large relative to the models normal error. We take the last 120 days and inject three real problems: a sign-up outage (one day at 40% of normal), a tracking break (ten days at 80% of normal) and a bot spike (one day at 180%). The holiday period at the end of the year is a genuine, expected dip that should not be flagged. window = signups.index[-120:] observed = signups.copy() truth = pd.Series(False, index=signups.index) for day, factor in [("2025-09-17", 0.4), ("2025-11-04", 1.8)]: observed[day] *= factor; truth[day] = True brk = pd.date_range("2025-10-08", periods=10) observed[brk] *= 0.8; truth[brk] = True # Model fitted on history before the monitoring window, predicting each day in it hist = observed[:window[0] - pd.Timedelta(days=1)] model = sm.OLS(np.log1p(hist), design(hist.index)).fit() resid = np.log1p(observed[window]) - model.predict(design(window)) mad = np.median(np.abs(model.resid - np.median(model.resid))) * 1.4826 # robust scale robust_z = resid / mad rules = { "Day-over-day change > 25%": (observed.pct_change().abs() > 0.25)[window], "Same weekday last week, change > 25%": (observed.pct_change(7).abs() > 0.25)[window], "Model residual, |robust z| > 3": (robust_z.abs() > 3), } rows = [] for name, flag in rules.items(): tp = (flag & truth[window]).sum() rows.append({"rule": name, "days flagged": int(flag.sum()), "true problems caught": int(tp), "false alarms": int((flag & ~truth[window]).sum()), "problem days": int(truth[window].sum())}) print(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("rule").to_string()) ## days flagged true problems caught false alarms problem days ## rule ## Day-over-day change > 25% 38 5 33 12 ## Same weekday last week, change > 25% 25 6 19 12 ## Model residual, |robust z| > 3 6 6 0 12 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8)) expected = np.expm1(model.predict(design(window))) ax.plot(window, observed[window], lw=1, color="#333", label="Observed") ax.plot(window, expected, lw=1.5, ls="--", label="Expected") flagged = window[rules["Model residual, |robust z| > 3"].values] ax.scatter(flagged, observed[flagged], color="#C8102E", zorder=3, s=20, label="Flagged") for d in window[truth[window].values]: ax.axvspan(d - pd.Timedelta(hours=12), d + pd.Timedelta(hours=12), color="#9A5B00", alpha=0.15, lw=0) ax.set_ylabel("Daily sign-ups") ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 20.1: Monitoring window: observed sign-ups, the models expectation, and days flagged by the residual rule. Injected problems are shaded. The day-over-day rule drowns real problems in weekend alarms. The week-over-week rule is quieter but still fires on holidays and again a week after each problem, because last weeks anomaly becomes this weeks baseline. The model-based rule ignores the weekly pattern and the holidays, because it expects them, and flags the outage and spike. A modest tracking break is the hardest case: each day is only 20% low, so single-day thresholds catch only some of its days. Shifts that persist are better caught by change-point methods on the residuals or on ratios such as tracked to backend conversions (Chapter 2), which accumulate evidence over several days. Good monitoring combines both: a residual rule for sharp one-day problems, and a change-point or cumulative-sum check for level shifts, run per market and per channel, with alerts routed to someone who can act. 20.5 Tools Classical: statsmodels (ETS, SARIMAX, regression with Fourier terms), the forecast and fable packages in R. Prophet and NeuralProphet: decomposable trend-seasonality-holiday models, easy to set up for business data. Nixtlas statsforecast and neuralforecast: fast implementations of many models, convenient for backtesting at scale. Foundation models such as Chronos: pretrained forecasters that can work without fitting; worth backtesting against the simple baselines before relying on them. Anomaly and change-point detection: ruptures, adtk, Kats, Rbeast. 20.6 Checklist Is every forecast compared with a seasonal naive baseline in a rolling-origin backtest at the relevant horizon? Do prediction intervals achieve close to their nominal coverage in the backtest? Are holidays, promotions and known events in the model, so that expected dips are not treated as surprises? Do monitoring alerts compare each day with a model expectation, scaled by the models normal error, rather than with yesterday? Are persistent level shifts checked with change-point or cumulative methods, not only single-day thresholds? Is each alert routed to an owner, with the change log checked before escalating? 20.7 Further reading Forecasting: Principles and Practice (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos) and its Python read-along; skforecast, Greykite (LinkedIn) and Orbit (Uber). Chapter 21 Paid search How much of paid search is incremental, especially on brand terms, how to set bids and budgets on marginal rather than average cost, and which tests settle the question. 21.1 Why search needs special care Paid search captures demand rather than creating most of it. People who search for your brand were already looking for you; people who search for the category are already in the market. That makes search look excellent in attribution (Chapter 13) and dangerous in an MMM (Chapter 9), where its spend moves with demand. The two questions that matter are how much of it is incremental, and what the next euro buys. 21.2 Brand terms: how much would you get anyway? When you stop bidding on your own brand name, many of the people who would have clicked the ad click the organic result instead. The incremental value of brand search is the share of traffic that does not come back, plus whatever protection the ads give against competitors bidding on your name. Both vary by market and by how aggressively competitors bid, so it has to be measured. A clean design is a switchback test across regions: randomly assign each region-week to brand ads on or off, so that every region spends some weeks in each state, and compare total brand-search visits (paid plus organic). 21.2.1 Worked example Twenty regions, twelve weeks, brand ads on or off at random each region-week. Without ads, 80% of brand searches end in an organic click. With ads on, the ad takes half of those clicks and adds a small number of visits that would not have happened otherwise (8% of searches). So roughly five in six paid brand clicks would have arrived organically anyway. import numpy as np, pandas as pd, warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import statsmodels.formula.api as smf rng = np.random.default_rng(21) R, W = 20, 12 rows = [] size = rng.lognormal(np.log(2000), 0.5, R) week_effect = 1 + 0.08 * np.sin(np.arange(W) / 2) for r in range(R): for w in range(W): on = int(rng.random() < 0.5) searches = rng.poisson(size[r] * week_effect[w]) organic_without_ads = rng.binomial(searches, 0.80) incremental = rng.binomial(searches, 0.08) if on else 0 # visits only the ad produces captured = rng.binomial(organic_without_ads, 0.5) if on else 0 # would-be organic clicks taken by the ad rows.append({"region": r, "week": w, "ads_on": on, "paid_clicks": captured + incremental, "visits": organic_without_ads + incremental}) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) df["log_visits"] = np.log(df["visits"]) fit = smf.ols("log_visits ~ ads_on + C(region) + C(week)", df).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["region"]}) lift = np.exp(fit.params["ads_on"]) - 1 lo, hi = np.exp(fit.conf_int().loc["ads_on"]) - 1 on = df[df.ads_on == 1] incr_visits = on["visits"].sum() * lift / (1 + lift) print(f"Brand-search visits with ads on vs off: {lift:+.1%} (95% CI {lo:+.1%} to {hi:+.1%})") ## Brand-search visits with ads on vs off: +9.8% (95% CI +9.0% to +10.6%) print(f"Paid brand clicks in 'on' weeks: {on['paid_clicks'].sum():,.0f}; implied incremental visits: {incr_visits:,.0f} " f"({incr_visits / on['paid_clicks'].sum():.0%} of paid clicks)") ## Paid brand clicks in 'on' weeks: 144,237; implied incremental visits: 23,557 (16% of paid clicks) Total brand-search visits are only about 10% higher with ads on, and only about one paid brand click in six is incremental. If brand CPC is 0.30 EUR, the cost per incremental visit is around six times that. Whether brand bidding pays depends on that incremental cost against the value of a visit, and on what competitors do in your absence. Those are empirical questions, and the answer differs between markets: where competitors bid aggressively on your name, the incremental share is much higher. Turning brand search off nationally for two weeks and comparing with the two weeks before. Seasonality, other campaigns and competitor moves all change in the same window. Randomize across regions and weeks, and measure total brand traffic, not paid clicks. 21.3 Non-brand terms: marginal, not average For non-brand terms, the issue is less incrementality (most non-brand clicks would not have reached you otherwise) than diminishing returns. Raising bids buys more clicks at higher prices; each extra conversion costs more than the last. Search platforms bid simulators, or your own spend tests, trace a curve of conversions against spend. A power curve, conversions \(= a \cdot \text{spend}^b\) with \(b < 1\), usually fits well. a, b = 0.8, 0.62 # fitted from bid-simulator points, for example spend = np.array([5_000, 10_000, 20_000, 30_000, 40_000, 60_000]) conv = a * spend ** b avg_cpa = spend / conv marg_cpa = 1 / (a * b * spend ** (b - 1)) # derivative of spend w.r.t. conversions print(pd.DataFrame({"monthly spend": spend, "conversions": conv.round(0), "average CPA": avg_cpa.round(0), "marginal CPA": marg_cpa.round(0)}).to_string(index=False)) ## monthly spend conversions average CPA marginal CPA ## 5000 157.0 32.0 51.0 ## 10000 242.0 41.0 67.0 ## 20000 371.0 54.0 87.0 ## 30000 477.0 63.0 101.0 ## 40000 571.0 70.0 113.0 ## 60000 734.0 82.0 132.0 The marginal CPA is always above the average CPA, by a factor of \(1/b\) (here about 1.6). A team managing to an average CPA target of 60 EUR will keep raising spend until the average reaches 60, by which point the last conversions cost close to 100 EUR each. Set targets on marginal CPA, equal across campaigns and markets, and equal to what an incremental conversion is worth (Chapter 12). 21.4 Smart bidding and automated campaigns Automated bidding and campaign types that span many inventories (such as Performance Max) optimize toward the conversions the platform can see, using signals including brand searches and remarketing audiences. They will find the cheapest attributed conversions, which are often the least incremental: brand-term traffic and existing customers. Practical safeguards: Separate brand and non-brand in reporting and, where the platform allows, in campaigns, so that cheap brand conversions do not subsidize the reported CPA of everything else. Feed value, not just conversions: offline conversion uploads with the system-of-record outcome and its value (Chapter 2), so the algorithm optimizes toward customers that matter. Exclude existing customers from acquisition campaigns where possible. Measure with geo tests or conversion lift studies (Chapters 6 and 8), not with the campaigns own attribution. 21.5 Checklist Is brand search incrementality measured with a randomized design (regional switchback or geo holdout) on total brand traffic? Are brand and non-brand reported and targeted separately? Are bids and budgets set on marginal CPA, not average CPA? Do automated campaigns receive system-of-record conversions and values, and exclude existing customers? Is the search channels MMM estimate treated as likely upward-biased until calibrated (Chapter 11)? 21.6 Further reading What am I willing to pay per click?, Bid simulator and marginal CPA and Paid search optimal bid (VexPower and others in the library). Chapter 22 Paid social and creative fatigue Whether paid social prospecting is incremental, how to test creatives fairly, and when a creative has worn out and needs replacing. 22.1 What makes paid social different Paid social platforms sell attention in feeds, and their delivery algorithms decide who sees which ad. Three consequences shape how it should be measured. The platform chooses the audience. Optimization toward conversions sends ads to people the algorithm predicts will convert, many of whom would have converted anyway. Attributed conversions overstate incrementality, often by a large factor (Chapters 1 and 8). Creative is the main lever. With targeting increasingly automated, the creative does most of the work of reaching the right people and persuading them. Creative testing and refresh are where much of the performance comes from. Effects extend beyond the click. Video and upper-funnel formats drive branded search, direct visits and later conversions that the platform cannot see. Lift studies on platform outcomes and geo tests on backend outcomes (Chapter 6) see different parts of this. For incrementality, use the platforms conversion lift studies with system-of-record conversions where possible, and geo tests for the biggest budget decisions. The rest of this chapter is about creative. 22.2 Testing creatives fairly Putting several creatives in one ad set and comparing their results is not a test. The delivery algorithm shifts spend toward whichever creative looks better in its first impressions, gives the others little delivery, and shows them to different audiences. The comparison is confounded by who saw what and when, and early noise becomes a self-fulfilling verdict. A fair creative test needs: Randomized audiences: the platforms split-test or A/B feature, which assigns users to cells and holds delivery comparable. A metric that matters: cost per acquired customer (or better, per incremental customer), not click-through rate. Creatives that maximize clicks are often not the ones that convert. Enough volume and a fixed duration, set from the expected difference and the baseline rate (Chapter 5). 22.3 Creative fatigue As the same people see the same creative again and again, response falls. That decline is fatigue, and its rate determines how often new creative is needed. It is best measured against frequency (average impressions per person reached), not calendar time, because a creative with a big budget wears out faster than the same creative with a small one. 22.3.1 Worked example: estimating how fast response decays Twelve creatives run for 60 days each, launched at different times, with different budgets and different baseline appeal. Each creatives click-through rate falls exponentially with its average frequency. We estimate the decay rate across all creatives at once with a Poisson regression of clicks on frequency, with a separate baseline for each creative and impressions as exposure. import numpy as np, pandas as pd, warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import statsmodels.api as sm import statsmodels.formula.api as smf rng = np.random.default_rng(22) K_TRUE = 0.18 # CTR falls by this rate per unit of average frequency rows = [] for c in range(12): base_ctr = rng.uniform(0.006, 0.015) daily_imps = rng.uniform(20_000, 80_000) audience = rng.uniform(150_000, 400_000) cum = 0.0 for d in range(60): imps = rng.poisson(daily_imps) cum += imps reach = audience * (1 - np.exp(-cum / audience)) freq = cum / reach # average frequency so far clicks = rng.binomial(imps, base_ctr * np.exp(-K_TRUE * (freq - 1))) rows.append({"creative": c, "day": d, "impressions": imps, "clicks": clicks, "frequency": freq}) ads = pd.DataFrame(rows) fit = smf.glm("clicks ~ C(creative) + frequency", ads, family=sm.families.Poisson(), offset=np.log(ads["impressions"])).fit() k = -fit.params["frequency"] lo, hi = -fit.conf_int().loc["frequency"][::-1] print(f"Estimated decay per unit of frequency: {k:.3f} (95% CI {lo:.3f} to {hi:.3f}); true {K_TRUE}") ## Estimated decay per unit of frequency: 0.179 (95% CI 0.177 to 0.181); true 0.18 print(f"CTR halves after about {np.log(2) / k:.1f} additional impressions per person") ## CTR halves after about 3.9 additional impressions per person print(f"CTR falls to 60% of launch level at an average frequency of about {1 + np.log(1 / 0.6) / k:.1f}") ## CTR falls to 60% of launch level at an average frequency of about 3.9 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ads["rel_ctr"] = ads["clicks"] / ads["impressions"] / np.exp( fit.params["Intercept"] + fit.params.filter(like="C(creative)").reindex( [f"C(creative)[T.{c}]" for c in ads["creative"]]).fillna(0).to_numpy() - k) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.7)) ax.scatter(ads["frequency"], ads["rel_ctr"], s=6, alpha=0.4, color="#6B6B6B") f = np.linspace(1, ads["frequency"].max(), 100) ax.plot(f, np.exp(-k * (f - 1)), lw=2.2, color="#1F4E79", label="Estimated decay") ax.axhline(0.6, ls=":", color="#C8102E", label="Refresh threshold (60%)") ax.set_xlabel("Average frequency") ax.set_ylabel("CTR relative to launch") ax.legend() plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 22.1: Daily CTR relative to each creatives launch level, against average frequency, with the estimated decay curve. The pooled model recovers the true decay rate and turns it into a rule that planners can use: refresh a creative when its audiences average frequency approaches the threshold. Because the rule is in terms of frequency, it automatically schedules earlier refreshes for creatives with larger budgets or smaller audiences. Three cautions apply. Click-through is a convenient proxy, but fatigue in conversion rate or cost per acquisition is what matters, and it is noisier; check that the two move together before relying on clicks. Fatigue rates differ by format, audience and market, so estimate them on your own data and refresh the estimate. And frequency is not only a fatigue problem: some exposure is needed before response appears at all, so the right frequency is a balance, best found with tests of different frequency caps. Declaring a winning creative from an ad set where the algorithm chose the delivery. Use the platforms split-testing feature, or a holdout design, and judge on acquisition cost, not click-through. 22.4 Checklist Is paid social incrementality measured with lift studies on system-of-record outcomes, and checked with geo tests for large budgets? Are creative tests run with randomized audiences, on acquisition metrics, with a fixed sample size? Is fatigue measured against frequency rather than calendar days, with a refresh threshold derived from your own data? Do click-based fatigue signals agree with conversion-based ones? Are frequency caps tested rather than set by convention? 22.5 Further reading Creative fatigue analyses in the library, including Facebook ad fatigue (Enginescout), Find unicorn ads and avoid creative fatigue (MarTech Series) and Paid social creative testing blueprint (Kitchn). Chapter 23 SEO measurement Whether a change to your site (titles, templates, internal linking, content, technical fixes) improved organic search traffic, given that search engines change their rankings constantly and nobody can randomize users. 23.1 Why SEO is hard to measure Organic search traffic is driven by rankings you do not control. Search engines update their algorithms many times a year, competitors change their pages, seasonality moves demand, and your own other changes overlap. A before-and-after comparison on the pages you changed attributes all of that to your change. And you cannot randomize users, because the search engine decides what every user sees. What you can randomize is pages. If a site has many pages of the same type (product pages, location pages, help articles, blog posts), randomly assign some to receive the change and keep the rest as controls. Both groups experience the same algorithm updates, seasonality and competition; the difference in how their traffic changes estimates the effect. 23.2 Worked example: an SEO split test A site has 400 pages of the same template. On day 90, a new title format goes live on 200 randomly chosen pages, and truly lifts their organic clicks by 6%. On day 80, a search engine update independently lifts traffic on all pages by about 10%, and the sites traffic is seasonally rising anyway. import numpy as np, pandas as pd, warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") rng = np.random.default_rng(23) P, T, LAUNCH, UPDATE, LIFT = 400, 120, 90, 80, 0.06 page_base = rng.lognormal(np.log(40), 0.9, P) # daily clicks per page day = np.arange(T) common = (1 + 0.002 * day) * (1 - 0.15 * np.isin(day % 7, [5, 6])) * np.where(day >= UPDATE, 1.10, 1.0) treated = np.zeros(P, bool) treated[rng.permutation(P)[: P // 2]] = True effect = np.where(treated[:, None] & (day[None, :] >= LAUNCH), 1 + LIFT, 1.0) page_noise = np.exp(np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.01, (P, T)), axis=1)) # pages drift independently clicks = rng.poisson(page_base[:, None] * common[None, :] * page_noise * effect) pre, post = slice(50, LAUNCH), slice(LAUNCH, T) before = clicks[:, pre].mean(1); after = clicks[:, post].mean(1) naive = after[treated].sum() / before[treated].sum() - 1 # Difference-in-differences on page-level log ratios, with a bootstrap over pages log_ratio = np.log((after + 1) / (before + 1)) did = lambda idx: np.exp(log_ratio[idx][treated[idx]].mean() - log_ratio[idx][~treated[idx]].mean()) - 1 est = did(np.arange(P)) boot = [did(rng.integers(0, P, P)) for _ in range(2000)] print(f"Naive before/after on changed pages: {naive:+.1%}") ## Naive before/after on changed pages: +19.8% print(f"Split test (DiD vs control pages): {est:+.1%} (95% CI {np.quantile(boot, .025):+.1%} to " f"{np.quantile(boot, .975):+.1%}); true {LIFT:+.0%}") ## Split test (DiD vs control pages): +5.8% (95% CI +4.6% to +7.0%); true +6% import matplotlib.pyplot as plt idx = lambda m: pd.Series(clicks[m].sum(0) / clicks[m][:, pre].sum(0).mean()).rolling(7, center=True).mean() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.7)) ax.plot(day, idx(treated), lw=2, label="Changed pages") ax.plot(day, idx(~treated), lw=2, ls="--", label="Control pages") ax.axvline(UPDATE, ls=":", color="#6B6B6B") ax.text(UPDATE + 1, ax.get_ylim()[0] + 0.01, "algorithm update", fontsize=8) ax.axvline(LAUNCH, color="#C8102E", lw=1) ax.text(LAUNCH + 1, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 0.04, "change live", fontsize=8, color="#C8102E") ax.set_xlabel("Day") ax.set_ylabel("Clicks (pre-period = 1)") ax.legend(loc="upper left") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 23.1: Organic clicks for changed and control pages (7-day averages, indexed to the pre-period). The algorithm update moves both groups; only the title change separates them. The naive comparison credits the change with the algorithm update and the seasonal rise, and reports an effect several times too large. The split test differences them out and recovers the true lift with an honest interval. 23.3 Designing SEO tests Page groups must be comparable: same template, similar traffic profile. Randomize within strata of traffic (for example, pair pages by pre-period clicks and randomize within each pair) to improve balance and power. Enough pages and traffic. Page-level traffic is highly variable; dozens of pages with little traffic each will rarely detect a realistic effect. Run a placebo analysis on historical data first (pretend a change happened, as in Chapter 7) to see what effect size the design can detect. Allow for crawling and indexing. Search engines take days to weeks to re-crawl and re-rank changed pages. Define the readout window from launch plus indexing time, and check in the search console when changed pages were recrawled. Watch for spillover. Changes to internal linking or site-wide elements affect control pages too. Those changes need a site-level design (CausalImpact against other sites or markets, Chapter 7) rather than a page split. 23.4 Data caveats Search console data is aggregated and partly anonymized: rare queries are hidden, figures are rounded, and query-level and page-level totals do not always reconcile. Use page-level clicks for tests, keep the extraction method fixed, and log search engine updates and your own site releases in the change log (Chapter 2), because they are the most common confounders in organic traffic analysis. Attributing an organic traffic change to an SEO project without a comparison group. Algorithm updates, seasonality and competitor changes routinely move organic traffic by more than any single change you make. 23.5 Checklist Can the change be tested by randomizing comparable pages into changed and control groups? Is randomization stratified by pre-period traffic, and has a placebo analysis shown the design can detect a realistic effect? Does the readout window allow for crawling and re-ranking? Are site-wide changes analyzed with a site-level quasi-experiment instead of a page split? Are search engine updates and site releases in the change log? 23.6 Further reading Measuring SEO effectiveness using causal impact analysis (WordLift) with its Colab notebook; CausalImpact for SEO (JC Chouinard); SEO title tag optimization (Etsy engineering). Chapter 24 CRM and email holdouts Whether lifecycle messaging (email, push, in-app, SMS) actually changes customer behavior, which programs and messages to keep, and how to measure them when opens and clicks no longer mean what they used to. 24.1 Why CRM measurement is easy to get wrong CRM messages go to people who are already customers or prospects, and the people who engage with them are disproportionately the ones who were going to act anyway. Conversions from users who clicked the email is the purest form of the attribution problem from Chapter 13: engaged users click and convert, and the email takes the credit. Engagement metrics have also degraded. Mail clients that pre-fetch images (Apples Mail Privacy Protection is the best-known example) register opens that never happened, so open rates are inflated and no longer comparable over time or across audiences. Clicks are more reliable but still measure engagement, not effect. The good news is that CRM is the easiest channel to randomize. You control who receives each message, so every program can have a holdout. 24.2 Worked example: attributed versus incremental An onboarding email program goes to 50,000 new customers, with 20% randomly held out for the programs duration. The outcome is activation (first real use of the product) within 30 days. Customers differ in underlying intent; high-intent customers activate more often and click emails more often. The programs true effect is a modest increase in activation. import numpy as np, pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(24) n = 50_000 intent = rng.normal(0, 1, n) holdout = rng.random(n) < 0.20 p_base = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-0.8 + 1.2 * intent))) # activation without emails TRUE_EFFECT = 0.03 # +3 points for those who receive the program activated = rng.random(n) < np.where(holdout, p_base, np.clip(p_base + TRUE_EFFECT, 0, 1)) clicked = ~holdout & (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-1.5 + 1.0 * intent)))) attributed = (activated & clicked).sum() # "activated after clicking an email" rate_send, rate_hold = activated[~holdout].mean(), activated[holdout].mean() incremental = (rate_send - rate_hold) * (~holdout).sum() se = np.sqrt(rate_send * (1 - rate_send) / (~holdout).sum() + rate_hold * (1 - rate_hold) / holdout.sum()) print(f"Activation: send group {rate_send:.1%}, holdout {rate_hold:.1%}, " f"difference {rate_send - rate_hold:+.1%} (95% CI {rate_send - rate_hold - 1.96*se:+.1%} to " f"{rate_send - rate_hold + 1.96*se:+.1%})") ## Activation: send group 37.5%, holdout 35.3%, difference +2.2% (95% CI +1.2% to +3.3%) print(f"Attributed activations (clicked, then activated): {attributed:,}") ## Attributed activations (clicked, then activated): 4,673 print(f"Incremental activations (vs holdout): {incremental:,.0f}") ## Incremental activations (vs holdout): 895 print(f"Attributed / incremental: {attributed / incremental:.1f}x") ## Attributed / incremental: 5.2x The program works: activation is about two points higher in the send group (the true effect is three), and the holdout comparison says so with a usable interval. But activated after clicking overstates its contribution several times over, because clickers are the customers most likely to activate anyway. A program judged on attributed numbers looks like a large win; judged on the holdout, it is a real but modest one. That difference decides how much to invest in it, and whether a more ambitious program would pay. 24.3 Holdout designs for CRM Per-campaign holdouts: a random 5% to 20% of each sends audience receives nothing. Good for testing individual campaigns, but many small campaigns each have little power. Program-level holdouts: a random share of customers excluded from an entire program (onboarding, re-engagement) for its full duration. Measures the programs total effect, which is usually what decisions are about. Global holdout: a small, persistent random group (often 2% to 5%) that receives no marketing messages at all, refreshed periodically. Measures the cumulative effect of all CRM over months, including fatigue and unsubscribes, which campaign-level tests miss. Message tests within the send group: A/B tests between versions, with the holdout still in place, so you learn both which version is better and whether either beats nothing. Size the holdout from the effect you need to detect. Activation effects of a few percentage points need thousands of customers in the holdout; effects on revenue per customer, which is far noisier, need more (Chapter 5). from scipy import stats z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975) + stats.norm.ppf(0.8) p = 0.35 rows = [] for audience in [10_000, 50_000, 200_000]: for share in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20]: n_h, n_s = audience * share, audience * (1 - share) rows.append({"audience": f"{audience:,}", "holdout share": f"{share:.0%}", "MDE (points)": round(100 * z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / n_h + 1 / n_s)), 2)}) tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="audience", columns="holdout share", values="MDE (points)") print(tbl.loc[["10,000", "50,000", "200,000"], ["5%", "10%", "20%"]].to_string()) ## holdout share 5% 10% 20% ## audience ## 10,000 6.13 4.45 3.34 ## 50,000 2.74 1.99 1.49 ## 200,000 1.37 1.00 0.75 With small audiences and small holdouts, only large effects are detectable. Many CRM programs have true effects of one or two points; for them, a 5% holdout on 10,000 customers is unlikely to show anything, and the honest conclusion from a null result is we could not detect an effect smaller than about six points. Using open rates or conversions after click to evaluate CRM. Opens are inflated by privacy features; clicks select engaged users. Use randomized holdouts and measure the outcome itself. 24.4 Guardrails and long-term effects Messages have costs that a single campaign readout misses: unsubscribes and spam complaints remove people from future reach, and message fatigue can lower response to everything that follows. Track unsubscribe and complaint rates as guardrail metrics in every test, and use the global holdout to see the net effect of the whole program over months. A campaign that wins its own test while raising unsubscribes can still lose overall. Also watch for targeting by uplift rather than by engagement (Chapter 16): the customers most likely to respond to a re-engagement message are not always the least engaged ones, and some highly engaged customers react negatively to extra messages. 24.5 Checklist Does every CRM program have a randomized holdout, sized from the effect that matters? Is there a persistent global holdout measuring the cumulative effect of all messaging? Are results read on the outcome (activation, transactions, revenue), not on opens or post-click conversions? Are unsubscribes, complaints and long-run engagement tracked as guardrails? Are message A/B tests run with a no-message holdout still in place? 24.6 Further reading Email playbook (Za-zu) for program structure. Measurable hold-out group performance and A/B testing measured in revenue in the predictive marketing capability checklist in the library. Chapter 25 Readouts that change decisions How to write up an analysis or experiment so that the people who decide can act on it correctly: what to say first, how to state uncertainty without hedging, and how to report results that are weak, null or mixed. 25.1 The readout is part of the method An analysis that is right but misread has the same effect as one that is wrong. Most measurement failures in practice are not statistical errors but communication ones: a non-significant result reported as a small win, an interval dropped on the way into a slide, an observational estimate presented with the authority of an experiment, a caveat buried on page four that would have changed the decision. The structure below works for experiment readouts, model results and ad-hoc did it work? answers alike. 25.2 A structure that works The verdict and how sure you are, in one or two sentences. The heavy-up paid back with an iROAS of about 1.4, but the test cannot rule out a loss (95% interval 0.3 to 2.4). The reader who stops here should still make the right decision. What we did. Design (experiment, quasi-experiment, model, observational), dates, markets, sample, primary metric and its window. Two to five lines. Results. The primary metric with its interval, then secondary metrics and guardrails, in a table. Every number has a source. What we checked. Data quality, sample ratio, pre-period fit, placebo tests, sensitivity. One line each, with the outcome. Caveats that could change the conclusion. Not a list of every limitation; only those that would change what the reader should do. Recommendation. What to do, who owns it, by when, and what would change the recommendation. The order matters. Leading with method and caveats and ending with the answer protects the analyst and fails the reader. 25.3 Saying how sure you are Uncertainty is part of the result, not a disclaimer. A few conventions keep it precise without hedging every sentence. Always give the interval with the estimate, and say what the interval is (95% confidence, 90% credible). Lift 3.8% (95% CI 0.8% to 6.6%). Say what the result rules out. The test rules out a lift above 7% is often more useful than the point estimate. Report null results as results. We could not detect an effect; the test could have detected effects of 4% or more is a finding. A small positive lift (not significant) is not; it invites the reader to treat noise as signal. Name the designs strength. Experiments, quasi-experiments and models deserve different levels of confidence (Chapter 3). Say which one this is in the first paragraph. Disclose the analysis path. How many metrics and segments were examined, whether the test was read before its planned end, and whether the analysis plan changed. These change how much the result should be trusted (Chapter 5). A simple language ladder helps keep wording consistent across a team: Evidence Wording Interval excludes zero, design is an experiment X increased Y by about Z (interval) Interval excludes zero, quasi-experimental or model-based X is associated with an increase of about Z; the design cannot rule out [named confounders] Interval includes zero, test well powered We found no effect larger than [MDE] Interval includes zero, test underpowered The test was too small to tell; effects below [MDE] were undetectable 25.4 Showing uncertainty in charts Bar charts of point estimates hide exactly what the reader needs. Show intervals. import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt segments = ["DE", "IT", "FR", "ES"] est = np.array([4.1, 2.6, 1.9, -0.8]) half = np.array([2.2, 3.1, 2.9, 3.4]) # half-width of 95% interval fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 2.7), sharey=False) a1.bar(segments, est, color="#1F4E79") a1.set_title("Point estimates only") a1.set_ylabel("Lift (%)") y = np.arange(4)[::-1] a2.errorbar(est, y, xerr=half, fmt="o", capsize=4, color="#1F4E79") a2.axvline(0, color="#6B6B6B", lw=0.8) a2.set_yticks(y, segments) a2.set_title("With 95% intervals") a2.set_xlabel("Lift (%)") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Figure 25.1: The same results twice. Left: bars of point estimates suggest a clear ranking. Right: estimates with 95% intervals show that only one effect is distinguishable from zero and the ranking is uncertain. The left chart invites a ranking of markets and a decision to cut Spain. The right chart shows that only Germanys effect is distinguishable from zero, that the four intervals overlap heavily, and that a country ranking would mostly reflect noise. With four countries examined, the chance of at least one spurious significant result is already about one in five; a cut by country should be labeled as exploratory unless it was planned. Other habits worth keeping: put the decision threshold (break-even, target CPA) on the chart; avoid dual axes; label units; and keep the same scale across charts that will be compared. 25.5 An example: two versions of the same readout Version A. The Q2 heavy-up test in 8 regions showed a +3.8% lift in sign-ups (p = 0.01), delivering 1,040 incremental conversions and an iROAS of 1.39. Recommend rolling out the higher spend level nationally. Version B. The heavy-up increased sign-ups in the test regions by about 4% (95% interval 1% to 7%), so the extra spend did drive some conversions. At 120 EUR per conversion, that is an iROAS of about 1.4, but the interval runs from 0.3 to 2.4, so we cannot rule out that the extra spend lost money. Design: stratified randomized geo test, 8 of 40 regions, 30 days, backend sign-ups, synthetic control with placebo-based intervals; pre-period fit 3.4% MAPE. Recommendation: keep the higher level in the test regions for another 30 days to narrow the interval, rather than rolling out nationally now (owner: channel lead; decision date: end of next month). A national roll-out at this spend level would be a bet with roughly a one-in-four chance of losing money. Version A is shorter and sounds more decisive, and it would lead to a decision the evidence does not support. Version B gives the same headline, the uncertainty that matters, and a recommendation proportionate to it. 25.6 Checklist Does the readout open with the verdict and the confidence in it? Is the design named in the first paragraph, with observational results labeled as such? Does every estimate have an interval, a sample size, a time window and a source? Are null results reported with the effect size that could have been detected? Are the number of comparisons and any interim looks disclosed? Do charts show intervals and decision thresholds? Does the recommendation have an owner, a date and a statement of what would change it? 25.7 Further reading Data visualization: Fundamentals of Data Visualization (Claus Wilke), Data to viz, and the Python and R graph galleries. Statistical Thinking for the 21st Century (Poldrack) on communicating uncertainty. The Google and Meta measurement playbooks for examples of readout conventions in industry. Chapter 26 The analysts toolkit Which tools and working habits make measurement work reliable and repeatable, and where newer tools (including AI assistants) help and where they need care. 26.1 Habits before tools Tools change every year; a few habits outlast them and prevent most of the errors described in this book. Write the plan before the data. Hypothesis, design, metric, window, decision rule (Chapter 5). A dated plan is the best defense against analyzing until something looks good. Simulate before you analyze. Every worked example in this book used data with a known truth. Do the same for your own designs: simulate data that looks like yours, with an effect you choose, and check that the method recovers it and how often it would detect it. It costs an afternoon and regularly saves a quarter. Keep a change log of tracking, naming, pricing, promotion and platform changes (Chapter 2). Make analyses reproducible. Code in version control, fixed random seeds, pinned package versions, and a record of which data snapshot an analysis used. The test: could someone else rerun it six months from now and get the same number? Separate exploration from confirmation. Exploratory slicing generates hypotheses; confirmatory analyses test pre-specified ones. Label which is which in every readout. 26.1.1 Simulation-based power, in a dozen lines The simulation habit generalizes the power calculations used throughout the book. Write a function that generates one dataset under the design and returns the analysis result; run it many times with and without an effect. import numpy as np def simulate_once(rng, effect, n_regions=30, n_treated=10, days=28, noise=0.08): """One geo test: daily outcomes per region, multiplicative effect in treated regions.""" base = rng.lognormal(np.log(100), 0.6, n_regions) treated = rng.permutation(n_regions) < n_treated pre = base * rng.lognormal(0, noise, n_regions) post = base * rng.lognormal(0, noise, n_regions) * np.where(treated, 1 + effect, 1.0) log_ratio = np.log(post / pre) return log_ratio[treated].mean() - log_ratio[~treated].mean() def power(effect, sims=2000, seed=0): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) null = np.array([simulate_once(rng, 0.0) for _ in range(sims)]) alt = np.array([simulate_once(rng, effect) for _ in range(sims)]) crit = np.quantile(np.abs(null), 0.95) # 5% false positive rate under the null return (np.abs(alt) > crit).mean() for e in [0.02, 0.05, 0.08]: print(f"True lift {e:.0%}: power {power(e):.0%}") ## True lift 2%: power 6% ## True lift 5%: power 20% ## True lift 8%: power 42% The answer is sobering, and typical: with 30 regions, 10 treated, and region-level noise of this size, even an 8% lift is detected less than half the time. Finding that out takes seconds before a test, and a quarter of wasted spend after one. More regions, a longer pre-period, or a bigger spend change would be needed. The same pattern works for any design in this book: change simulate_once to match how your data is generated and how you will analyze it. Because the null distribution comes from the same simulation, the false positive rate is correct by construction, even for analyses with no textbook formula. 26.2 The core stack Task Typical tools Notes Data access SQL on the warehouse (Databricks, BigQuery, Snowflake) Build the measurement panel once (Chapter 2) and reuse it Analysis Python (pandas, statsmodels, scipy) or R (tidyverse, fixest) Either is fine; use what the team can review Bayesian modeling PyMC, Stan, NumPyro; PyMC-Marketing, Meridian for MMM Chapters 10 to 12 Experiments Platform tools, in-house assignment, GeoLift, matched_markets, CausalPy Chapters 5 to 7 Forecasting statsmodels, Prophet, statsforecast, Chronos Always backtest against a seasonal naive (Chapter 20) Notebooks and reports Jupyter, marimo, Quarto, R Markdown, bookdown Reports generated from code stay in sync with the analysis Exploration sweetviz, DataExplorer, PyGWalker, naniar Quick profiling of new data before modeling Dashboards Looker Studio, Tableau, internal BI tools Show intervals and thresholds, not only point estimates Spreadsheets still have a place: quick break-even calculations, sharing small tables, and teaching. The librarys Google Sheets and Excel resources include regression, logistic regression, conjoint and pricing workbooks that are useful for explaining methods to non-analysts. 26.3 AI assistants in measurement work Large language model assistants are now part of most analysts workflow, and they are genuinely useful for drafting SQL and code, explaining unfamiliar methods, reviewing code for errors, generating simulation scaffolding, and writing first drafts of readouts. Text-to-SQL tools and AI analyst agents connected to a warehouse can answer routine questions quickly. They also fail in ways that matter specifically for measurement: Plausible but wrong definitions. An assistant will choose an industry-standard definition of a metric when your companys definition differs. Check generated queries against the metric dictionary. Silent analytical choices. Generated analyses make decisions (filters, windows, outlier handling, which comparison to make) without flagging them. Each one can change the answer. Confident causal language. Assistants readily describe correlations as effects and before-and-after comparisons as impact. Apply the same scrutiny as to any analysts draft (Chapter 25). Data handling. Customer and financial data should only go into tools approved for it. The practical rule is the same as for any junior collaborator: use them to go faster, review everything, and verify every number that will reach a decision against a source you trust. 26.4 Building a measurement teams library The resource library behind this book (Appendix A) is an example of a habit worth copying: a shared, organized collection of methods, tools, case studies and code that the team adds to as it learns. Pair it with an internal record of your own experiments and their results, with designs, dates, outcomes and what changed afterwards. Over time, that record becomes the most valuable measurement asset you have: priors for new models, benchmarks for new tests, and evidence of what actually works in your market. 26.5 Checklist Is there a written plan, dated before the data, for every confirmatory analysis? Was the design checked by simulation, including its power and false positive rate? Is the analysis reproducible: code in version control, seeds fixed, package versions and data snapshot recorded? Are AI-generated queries and analyses reviewed against the metric dictionary and checked for silent choices? Is there a shared record of past experiments and results that new work can draw on? 26.6 Further reading marimo, Quarto and bookdown for reproducible notebooks and reports; great_tables for publication-quality tables in Python. B Glossary Adstock The carryover of an advertising effect into later periods. Geometric adstock carries a fixed share of each periods effect into the next (Chapter 9). Attributed conversions Conversions a tracking rule assigns to a channel because the converting user was exposed to it. Not the same as incremental conversions (Chapters 1 and 13). Average versus marginal return Average return is total outcome per unit of total spend; marginal return is the extra outcome from the next unit of spend. Budget decisions depend on the marginal return (Chapter 12). Backtest (rolling-origin) Evaluating a forecast by repeatedly fitting on data up to a date and forecasting the following period, then moving the date forward (Chapter 20). Calibration (of an MMM) Using experiment results to constrain a models estimates, as a prior or an additional likelihood term (Chapter 11). Censoring Incomplete observation of a time-to-event outcome, such as customers who have not churned yet. Methods that ignore it are biased (Chapter 16). Cohort A group of customers acquired in the same period, usually also by the same channel, tracked by time since acquisition (Chapter 15). Collider A variable caused by two others. Conditioning on it creates a spurious association between them (Chapter 3). Confounder A common cause of the treatment and the outcome. Failing to adjust for it biases the estimated effect (Chapter 3). Conjoint analysis A survey method in which respondents choose between product profiles, used to estimate the value of features and willingness to pay (Chapter 19). Counterfactual What would have happened without the treatment. Every causal estimate compares an observed outcome with an estimated counterfactual (Chapter 3). CUPED A variance-reduction technique for experiments that adjusts outcomes using pre-experiment values of the same metric (Chapter 5). Difference-in-differences (DiD) Comparing the change over time in a treated group with the change in a comparison group, under the assumption of parallel trends (Chapter 7). Divergence (MCMC) A warning from Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samplers that the posterior geometry was not explored reliably, often fixed by reparameterization (Chapter 10). Double jeopardy The empirical regularity that smaller brands have fewer buyers who are also slightly less loyal (Chapter 18). Geo experiment An experiment that randomizes geographic regions rather than individuals to treatment and control (Chapter 6). Guardrail metric A metric that must not deteriorate in a test, such as unsubscribes or complaints, even if the primary metric improves (Chapters 5 and 24). Hazard ratio In survival models, the ratio of the instantaneous risk of the event between two groups. An association unless the grouping was randomized (Chapter 16). Holdout A randomly selected group deliberately not exposed to a treatment, used as the counterfactual (Chapters 8 and 24). iROAS, iCPA Incremental return on ad spend and incremental cost per acquisition: outcomes caused by the spend, per unit of spend, and spend per caused acquisition. Incrementality factor The ratio of incremental to attributed conversions measured in an experiment, used to adjust platform reporting (Chapter 8). Intent-to-treat (ITT) An effect estimated by comparing groups as randomized, regardless of whether each unit actually received the treatment (Chapter 8). Lifetime value (LTV) The expected margin a customer generates over a defined horizon, often discounted (Chapter 15). Marketing mix model (MMM) A regression model of a business outcome on media activity and other drivers over time, used for allocation and budget decisions (Chapters 9 to 12). Mediator A variable on the causal path from treatment to outcome. Adjusting for it removes part of the effect being measured (Chapter 3). Minimum detectable effect (MDE) The smallest true effect a design detects with a stated probability (usually 80%) at a stated significance level (Chapter 5). Multiple comparisons The inflation of false positives when many metrics, segments or tests are examined (Chapter 5). Parallel trends The assumption that treated and comparison groups would have followed parallel paths without treatment (Chapter 7). Peeking Checking an experiments result repeatedly and stopping when it looks significant, which inflates the false positive rate (Chapter 5). Placebo test Running an analysis where no effect should exist (a fake treatment date or fake treated units) to check the methods false positive rate (Chapters 6 and 7). Posterior predictive check Comparing data simulated from a fitted Bayesian model with the observed data. Necessary but not sufficient evidence of a good model (Chapter 10). Prior predictive check Simulating from the priors alone to check that they imply plausible outcomes before fitting (Chapters 4 and 10). Response curve Expected outcome as a function of spend in a channel, whose slope is the marginal return (Chapter 12). Sample ratio mismatch (SRM) A statistically significant difference between the planned and observed split of units in an experiment, indicating a broken assignment or logging (Chapter 5). Saturation Diminishing returns to spend within a period (Chapter 9). Share of search A brands share of branded search volume within its category, used as a leading indicator of market share (Chapter 18). Synthetic control A counterfactual built as a weighted combination of untreated units that tracks the treated unit before treatment (Chapters 6 and 7). Triangulation Combining evidence from several methods, with explicit allowances for each ones biases, to reach a decision (Chapter 14). Uplift The individual-level difference a treatment makes to an outcome. Targeting by uplift differs from targeting by predicted risk or engagement (Chapter 16).

C All checklists in one place Every chapter ends with a checklist. They are collected here for use as a pre-flight list before an analysis, a test or a readout. Each heading links back to the chapter that explains the items. What marketing science is for Chapter 1. What decision will this analysis inform, and who will make it? What would we do if the answer came out high? If it came out low? If both are the same, stop. Is the question about attributed, incremental or marginal performance? Is the method able to answer that question? Which evidence layer does the method belong to, and does a higher layer already disagree with it? What precision is needed for the decision, and can the planned design deliver it? Is there a tracking change, naming change or promotion in the window that would break a comparison? Data and signal foundations Chapter 2. Is the outcome taken from the system of record, not from tracking? Are tracked and backend outcomes stored side by side, with their ratio monitored? Is there a change log, and does any entry overlap the analysis window? Is unmapped spend below an agreed threshold for every week in the window? Have currency, time zone and duplicate checks been run? Does every channel you want to measure have enough spend variation to learn from? Are all channels included, including offline ones, so that omitted spend does not bias the rest? Causal thinking for marketers Chapter 3. Have you written down the counterfactual: what exactly would have happened without the treatment? Have you drawn the causal graph, including how the budget was set? Which variables are confounders (adjust) and which are mediators or colliders (do not adjust)? Does the analysis filter on anything that happens after treatment? Where on the identification ladder does the method sit, and is the decision large enough to justify climbing higher? Does the readout state the design, the uncertainty and the confounders that remain? Bayesian reasoning in practice Chapter 4. Are priors set and documented before fitting, with a source for each informative prior? Has a prior predictive check confirmed that the priors imply plausible outcomes? Has a sensitivity analysis shown whether a different reasonable prior changes the decision? When combining a model and an experiment, do they measure the same quantity (spend level, period, market, outcome)? Was the decision rule (thresholds on probability and expected loss) fixed before looking at results? Does the readout report probability of loss and expected loss, not just a point estimate? A/B tests that hold up Chapter 5. Is there a written plan with hypothesis, unit, primary metric and window, MDE, sample size, duration and decision rule, dated before launch? Does the MDE correspond to an effect size worth acting on? If not, redesign or do not run the test. Does the test run in whole weeks and long enough for the outcome window? Was the sample ratio checked, and were A/A tests run on this setup? Is the decision metric read only at the planned end, or under a pre-planned sequential design? How many comparisons does the readout make, and are they corrected or labeled as exploratory? Is a null result reported with the effect size that could have been detected? Geo experiments Chapter 6. Is the geo unit the smallest one at which media and outcomes can both be separated, with spillover considered? Was assignment randomized (ideally stratified), and is the method fixed in advance? Does a pre-test power analysis on historical data give an MDE worth testing for? Is the treatment type (go-dark, heavy-up, scale-back) matched to the decision (average versus marginal return)? Is delivery verified by region, so that the treatment actually happened as designed? Is the outcome taken from the system of record, with a cooldown window for lasting effects? Is the result reported as an iROAS range from placebo-based or model-based intervals, with the MDE? Quasi-experiments: DiD, CausalImpact and synthetic control Chapter 7. Is there a plausible comparison that was not affected by the intervention? For DiD: are event-study pre-period coefficients flat, and are standard errors clustered at the unit level? For staggered rollouts: is a staggered-adoption estimator used instead of plain two-way fixed effects? For CausalImpact: are the controls unaffected, chosen on pre-period grounds only, and fixed before looking? Do placebo-in-time (and, where possible, placebo-in-space) tests come out null? Does the change log show anything else hitting the treated unit in the window? Does the readout name the design as quasi-experimental and list the threats that remain? Reading platform lift studies Chapter 8. Is the outcome the platforms tracked conversion or your system-of-record conversion? Is the result intent-to-treat or per reached user, and does any comparison mix the two? How many conversions were in the holdout, and what MDE did the design have? Which confidence or credibility level is reported? Did budget, bidding or creative change during the study? Is the incrementality factor computed with its interval and stored with the conditions it was measured under (platform, campaign type, market, attribution setting, date)? If the result is applied to another market, campaign or spend level, is that stated as an assumption? Marketing mix modeling end to end Chapter 9. Is the outcome from the system of record, and are all major non-media drivers in the base? Does every modeled channel have meaningful spend variation (check the coefficient of variation), and are channels without it grouped or handled with priors? Is there a channel whose spend responds to demand (search, retargeting)? Treat its estimate as an upper bound until tested. Are adstock and saturation choices justified per channel type? Is the ratio of channels to observations reasonable, or is geo-level data available? Is anyone treating R or MAPE as validation? Bayesian MMM in practice Chapter 10. Is every prior written down with a reason, and does the prior predictive check imply plausible ROIs and media shares? Were divergences, R-hat and effective sample sizes checked before reading results? Does the posterior predictive check cover the data at roughly the nominal rate? For each channel, how does the posterior compare with the prior? Which channels are data-driven and which are prior-driven? Which channels spend responds to demand? Are their estimates flagged as likely upward-biased until tested? Validating and calibrating MMM Chapter 11. Has the model been refit on several windows, and are unstable channels flagged as unidentified? Is every channels estimate compared with an experiment where one exists? For channels whose spend responds to demand, is there a demand proxy that is a confounder (category level) rather than a mediator (brand level)? Are experiments used for calibration matched to the models outcome, market and spend level, with uncertainty inflated where they are not? Has parameter recovery been checked on data simulated to resemble the real situation? Is there an experiment plan for channels that remain unidentified? Response curves and budget optimization Chapter 12. Is the decision based on marginal ROI at current spend, not average ROI? Is the break-even threshold set on profit (margin-adjusted), not revenue? Are the curves from a calibrated model, and are channels with confounded or prior-dominated estimates flagged? Are optimizer bounds kept within the historically observed spend range? Is the expected gain reported with its uncertainty and the probability of a loss? Is the recommendation implemented as a measurable step (heavy-up or scale-back test) rather than all at once? Attribution and its limits Chapter 13. Is the attribution output being used to compare channels or set budgets? If so, stop and look for incrementality evidence. Are attributed conversions labeled as attributed in every report, never as incremental? For each channel, is its targeting correlated with existing intent (retargeting, CRM, branded search)? Expect over-credit. Where an incrementality factor exists, is it applied, with its date and conditions? How much of the journey is invisible because of consent, devices or platforms, and which channels does that hurt? Triangulation: deciding under contradictory evidence Chapter 14. Does each source have a stated bias allowance as well as its reported uncertainty? Is attribution kept out of incrementality combinations, or given a large allowance? Is the decision made on marginal returns, with probability and size of loss reported? Is the reversibility of the decision considered alongside expected value? Is the testing roadmap prioritized by money at stake and the chance of flipping a decision? Is there a channel scorecard with evidence type, age and confidence, kept up to date? Cohorts, retention, LTV and payback Chapter 15. Are retention and value analyzed by cohort (acquisition month and channel), not as blended averages? Does the retention model allow churn to fall as cohorts age, rather than assuming a constant rate? Is lifetime value built from margin, over a stated horizon, with discounting where the horizon is long? Is the uncertainty of projected LTV reported, and how much of it is projection beyond observed months? Are channel CAC targets set on value, and on incremental rather than attributed acquisition cost? For experiments that change customer mix, is value read at a long enough horizon? Churn and survival analysis Chapter 16. Are churn and lifetime estimated with methods that handle censoring (Kaplan-Meier, Cox, parametric survival), not averages over churned customers? Is the churn definition explicit and stable, with voluntary and involuntary churn separated? Are hazard ratios presented as associations unless the feature was randomized? Are retention offers targeted by uplift from a randomized test, rather than by predicted risk? Is the effect of retention interventions read at a horizon long enough to distinguish prevention from delay? Segmentation Chapter 17. Does each segment lead to a different, feasible action, and can a customers segment be identified when the action happens? Has a simple managerial segmentation (such as RFM) been tried as a baseline? Were features transformed and scaled deliberately, with the choice of what counts as different written down? Is the number of segments justified by actionability, with stability checked rather than silhouette alone? Are categorical features handled with an appropriate distance (Gower) rather than raw one-hot encoding? Are segments profiled on outcomes that were not clustering inputs, and are segment-specific treatments tested? Brand measurement Chapter 18. Is brand health tracked with a fixed set of metrics and a fixed competitor set, by market, over time? Is share of search used rather than raw branded search volume, and are changes rather than levels correlated? Is there a change log for events that move branded search (paid brand bidding, PR, incidents)? Are penetration and new-customer metrics tracked alongside loyalty metrics? Do performance experiments also record halo outcomes (branded search, direct, organic)? Are brand effects judged on windows long enough for them to appear? Pricing research and elasticities Chapter 19. Is the method matched to the decision: surveys for ranges and feature values, tests for final price changes? Are stated-intent results treated as relative signals, calibrated where possible against real conversion? Has the break-even volume change been calculated for the proposed price change at the actual margin? Are historical elasticities treated as confounded context rather than estimates? Does any price test respect fairness and regulatory constraints, and is it read on margin per customer over a long enough horizon, including mix effects? Forecasting and anomaly detection Chapter 20. Is every forecast compared with a seasonal naive baseline in a rolling-origin backtest at the relevant horizon? Do prediction intervals achieve close to their nominal coverage in the backtest? Are holidays, promotions and known events in the model, so that expected dips are not treated as surprises? Do monitoring alerts compare each day with a model expectation, scaled by the models normal error, rather than with yesterday? Are persistent level shifts checked with change-point or cumulative methods, not only single-day thresholds? Is each alert routed to an owner, with the change log checked before escalating? Paid search Chapter 21. Is brand search incrementality measured with a randomized design (regional switchback or geo holdout) on total brand traffic? Are brand and non-brand reported and targeted separately? Are bids and budgets set on marginal CPA, not average CPA? Do automated campaigns receive system-of-record conversions and values, and exclude existing customers? Is the search channels MMM estimate treated as likely upward-biased until calibrated (Chapter 11)? Paid social and creative fatigue Chapter 22. Is paid social incrementality measured with lift studies on system-of-record outcomes, and checked with geo tests for large budgets? Are creative tests run with randomized audiences, on acquisition metrics, with a fixed sample size? Is fatigue measured against frequency rather than calendar days, with a refresh threshold derived from your own data? Do click-based fatigue signals agree with conversion-based ones? Are frequency caps tested rather than set by convention? SEO measurement Chapter 23. Can the change be tested by randomizing comparable pages into changed and control groups? Is randomization stratified by pre-period traffic, and has a placebo analysis shown the design can detect a realistic effect? Does the readout window allow for crawling and re-ranking? Are site-wide changes analyzed with a site-level quasi-experiment instead of a page split? Are search engine updates and site releases in the change log? CRM and email holdouts Chapter 24. Does every CRM program have a randomized holdout, sized from the effect that matters? Is there a persistent global holdout measuring the cumulative effect of all messaging? Are results read on the outcome (activation, transactions, revenue), not on opens or post-click conversions? Are unsubscribes, complaints and long-run engagement tracked as guardrails? Are message A/B tests run with a no-message holdout still in place? Readouts that change decisions Chapter 25. Does the readout open with the verdict and the confidence in it? Is the design named in the first paragraph, with observational results labeled as such? Does every estimate have an interval, a sample size, a time window and a source? Are null results reported with the effect size that could have been detected? Are the number of comparisons and any interim looks disclosed? Do charts show intervals and decision thresholds? Does the recommendation have an owner, a date and a statement of what would change it? The analysts toolkit Chapter 26. Is there a written plan, dated before the data, for every confirmatory analysis? Was the design checked by simulation, including its power and false positive rate? Is the analysis reproducible: code in version control, seeds fixed, package versions and data snapshot recorded? Are AI-generated queries and analyses reviewed against the metric dictionary and checked for silent choices? Is there a shared record of past experiments and results that new work can draw on?
